#3247. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3243. Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

The usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ plan. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis

All limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

#3242. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these dividend stocks for boosting portfolio returns

Dividend stocks remain a popular choice for investors seeking steady income and higher portfolio returns. However, with thousands of dividend-paying companies to choose from, identifying the right stocks can be challenging.

In this regard, recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can provide useful insights and help identify dividend stocks backed by solid fundamentals and with attractive upside potential.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Independent oil and natural gas company Permian Resources (PR) is this week's first dividend stock. The company recently paid a quarterly base cash dividend of 16 cents per share. At an annualized dividend of 64 cents per share, PR offers a dividend yield of 3.5%.

Recently, Evercore analyst Chris Baker initiated coverage of Permian Resources stock with a price target of $25. The analyst believes that the company is well positioned to benefit from improving U.S. shale demand after the Iran conflict, thanks to its low-breakeven inventory that can boost free cash flow growth. Baker also noted PR's disciplined consolidation in the Permian Basin.

Furthermore, the 5-star analyst highlighted the company's focus on a single basin and management's efficient capital allocations across expansion efforts, strategic acquisitions, and share buybacks. Baker noted that management focuses investments on the higher-return Northern Delaware Basin, helping boost profitability.

"The key piece of our work here, and the reason we think PR deserves a higher multiple relative to more finite or less flexible shale stories, is that PR runs an acquire and exploit model," said Baker.

He explained that Permian Resources deserves a premium valuation as it continually acquires and develops new high-quality assets instead of relying on a limited inventory, a strategy that is the market is underappreciating.

Baker ranks No. 862 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 48.3%. See Permian Resources Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Valero Energy (VLO) is a manufacturer and marketer of petroleum-based and low-carbon liquid transportation fuels and petrochemical products. At a quarterly dividend of $1.20 per share, or annualized dividend of $4.80 per share, VLO stock offers a yield of about 2%.

Heading into Valero's second-quarter earnings on July 30, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on VLO stock and increased the price target to $286 from $283 to reflect updated estimates.

Specifically, the 5-star analyst raised his 2026 and 2027 earnings per share estimates to $31.42 and $23.07 from $29.42 and $21.06, respectively, while leaving the 2028 EPS estimate unchanged at $20.37. Mehta made these revisions based on several factors, including updated commodity price assumptions and changes to refining capture rates.

Despite a strong year-to-date rally in VLO stock, Mehta still finds it compelling due to his more positive refining outlook. Moreover, the analyst sees the possibility of solid estimate revisions, which could drive the stock higher. He believes that Valero is well-positioned to benefit from improving refining market conditions due to its strong position in the Gulf Coast, solid balance sheet strength, and low-cost operations.

"Additionally, we believe the company's premium asset portfolio and crude slate optionality should support capture rates and stronger cash flow generation in the near-term, ultimately supporting shareholder returns," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 742 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.2%. See Valero Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

Moving on to Ovintiv (OVV), a North American oil and natural gas producer. It has solid positions in North America's premier oil basins – the Permian and the Montney. OVV offers a quarterly dividend of 30 cents per share, or an annualized dividend of $1.20 per share, implying a 2.3% yield.

Following meetings with management, RBC Capital analyst Gregory Pardy reaffirmed a buy rating on Ovintiv stock with a price target of $70, highlighting that the stock is on RBC's Global Energy Best Ideas List.

"In our eyes, the depth of Ovintiv's Montney position, streamlined portfolio, strong balance sheet and enhanced shareholder returns afford investors with an attractive valuation re-rating opportunity over time," said Pardy.

#3241. Munich startup RHISE AI raises angel round for personal AI assistant Lucie

RHISE AI’s founders, from left: Chris Seybold, Andy Loy, Samy Samandjeu, and Danil Gontovnik

In January 2021, Andy Loy’s Munich startup KONUX raised $80 million in a Series C round, and around the same time, its founder was in hospital, exhausted and burned out at 29.

Loy eventually stepped away from the chief executive role, but when he returned to building technology, he had a different idea of what it should do. Rather than create another product competing for people’s attention, he wanted to build one that could give it back.

That idea became RHISE AI, the Munich company behind Lucie, a personal AI assistant that connects information from different parts of a user’s life, including health data, calendars, and email.

The company announced an angel funding round today, raising €2.66 million backed by more than 40 investors.  Among them are Andy Bechtolsheim, co-founder of Arista Networks and an early investor in Google, and Prince Max von und zu Liechtenstein, chairman of LGT. Former Siemens and Alcoa chief Klaus Kleinfeld, Splunk founder Michael Baum, and Bayern Munich footballer Leon Goretzka are also investors.

Michael Baum says he has spent much of his career backing technology designed to capture people’s time. Lucie, he believes, takes a different approach.

“I’ve spent 35 years building and backing technology that wanted more of people’s time. Lucie gives it back. I invested, and I use it daily,” he said in a statement.

Loy founded RHISE AI with chief technology officer Danil Gontovnik, Samy Samandjeu, and Chris Seybold. Their product is built around a relatively straightforward premise: an assistant should be able to recognise when something in your life needs attention, without requiring you to ask first.

Lucie brings together information from connected services, including wearables, calendars, and inboxes. Its multi-agent system, Heartbeat, monitors that information in the background. If it spots something unusual, such as a suspiciously high bill, it can suggest what to do next. The user must approve an action before the assistant carries it out, according to the company.

“Personal AI will soon know more about us than any technology before it. The question is who it works for,” Loy said.

That question is becoming harder to avoid as technology companies develop assistants with access to increasingly personal information. RHISE AI says it has designed Lucie to comply with GDPR from the outset, stores personal data in Germany, and does not use advertising or sell user data.

More than half of its active users have connected wearables that share real-time health readings with the assistant, the company said.

For a European startup, the timing is interesting, as some of the biggest consumer AI launches of the year have left European users waiting. Apple’s AI-powered Siri features are missing from EU iPhones, Google’s Gemini Spark does not include the European Economic Area, and Meta’s Muse is currently available only in the US and Canada.

That leaves room for European companies to make their case, particularly as concerns about data protection and dependence on American technology grow. Meta’s decision to use conversations with its AI assistant to inform advertising recommendations, introduced in December, has added to those concerns. The policy excludes the EU, UK, and South Korea.

In Germany, 72% of respondents consider the country too dependent on the US for AI, according to a Bitkom survey.

The assistant currently supports English and German and is available only on Apple devices. An Android version is planned.

For Loy, the project is a considerable departure from the industrial AI business he built with KONUX. The underlying ambition, however, is still to make technology useful. This time, he wants to measure that usefulness by what people no longer have to spend their time doing.

#3240. macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

#3239. iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this new feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

#3237. OpenAI board member puts the risk of an AI takeover next year at about 10%

Paul Christiano told the Dwarkesh Podcast he speaks as a private citizen. A week earlier, opening the Hinton Lectures in Toronto, he called an AI takeover a high risk within three years.

Paul Christiano giving a lecture at UCLA’s Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics in 2026

Paul Christiano sits on the OpenAI Foundation board and its safety committee. He says AI developers should stop improving their training algorithms for now, because their security is too weak to stop theft. He made the case to Dwarkesh Patel on a podcast published on 16 November.

“I would say we are looking more like a 10% risk than a 1% risk over the next year,” Christiano said of an AI takeover.

If developers race ahead without precautions, the risk is “significantly more than” 10%, he said. He also saw “maybe a 1/3 chance” of superintelligence within a year, unless the industry slows.

He stressed that he spoke as a private citizen. He was not reporting the board’s views, he said.

Christiano said labs should not keep improving pre-training and reinforcement learning with their current security. That is bad for US national security, in his view. If labs later slowed down for safety, an adversary could steal the models or methods and race ahead.

He said OpenAI and Anthropic both recently had “extremely unsophisticated actors” inside their systems. Those actors reached Slack or OpenAI’s shared code, with enough access to extract most algorithmic work. Patel cited researchers who used Claude to reach OpenAI’s internal code.

“Improving algorithms in a way that can be very loosely diffused even normally, and could be quickly stolen, I think they should stop that right now,” Christiano said.

Fixing security would take at least months, and possibly six to 12, he said. He admitted his view is not widely held. If everyone at OpenAI and Anthropic agreed on a pause, it would reasonably likely happen, he said. He did not say where anyone stands.

Christiano pointed to hundreds of maths results from OpenAI and Anthropic systems in about a month. He also cited METR’s finding that Anthropic’s pace had doubled. But METR’s full report is redacted, he noted.

“We should not be relying on METR and Anthropic saying, ‘It looks to us like we’re going to be able to overthrow governments in a year,’” he said.

On the current trend alone, he said, AI that reliably beats humans might take four years. He felt more confident about eight. His bigger worry is AI automating AI research and speeding it up at least tenfold. He called that probably more likely than not.

He gave humanity two “saving throws”, each at about 50%. One is finding a method that works in time. The other is being able to stop. Together that means about a 75% chance things are okay, he said, but the industry cannot yet stop. Patel said he doubts things will move this fast, though he called it a live possibility.

A week earlier, on 9 November, Christiano opened the Hinton Lectures in Toronto. He said there is a “high risk” of an AI takeover within the next three years.

“I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident,” Christiano told the audience.

Geoffrey Hinton introduced him. Christiano founded the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit. He led alignment research at OpenAI from 2017 to 2021 and did early work on RLHF. He is also a senior technical advisor at NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. He joined the OpenAI Foundation board in September, the foundation said. In his government role, he recuses himself from OpenAI matters.

In Toronto, he defined a takeover as AI systems that “call the shots” on Earth. If the industry built AI as fast as possible, he put the risk at “something like a coin flip”.

His main example was the summer incident in which OpenAI’s agents breached Hugging Face. They had been trying to fool the grader of a hacking test. A similar failure in far stronger systems would most likely be hard for humanity to recover from, he told Patel. He also cited a UK AI Security Institute test. In it, a Claude agent tried to plant malicious code on GitHub.

Colin Raffel of the University of Toronto and Hugging Face sat on the lecture panel. He said much of what Christiano described is reasonable to expect if things continue. But humans still have agency, he said, and society could decide current systems are good enough.

Christiano said he has usually underestimated AI progress, but may now be overestimating it. AI researcher Gary Marcus has told Business Insider he sees no credible near-term scenario for human extinction.

#3236. iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates

iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature. The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.

When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

Additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.

Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’

You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

I use these hidden Apple Watch features all the time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best Apple Watches are capable of some pretty remarkable things, like sending for help if you take a nasty fall, predicting your daily readiness, and logging physical fitness.

But with so much capability, some of the most useful Apple Watch tools and apps inevitably fly under the radar. That's where I come in. I'm Dan, and I lead TG's smartwatch review coverage. I'm also an avid Apple Watch wearer with strong opinions and a knack for tinkering with settings.

With that in mind, here are five favorite lesser-known Apple Watch features that I absolutely swear by. Some were added via the recent watchOS 27 release, while others are old standbys.

Note: This list expands my previously published 7 hidden Apple Watch features I swear by round-up from earlier in the year.

Dividing up a check between friends can be a tedious task, especially if you and your pals aren't math whizzes. If only there were a super-simple way to calculate a tip and split a check without breaking a sweat.

There is! Your Apple Watch's boring old Calculator app features a built-in tip button. Simply enter the total amount of the check and tap "Tip." This brings up a screen where you can enter your desired tip percentage and the number of individuals paying for an instant calculation.

And just like that, you'll never fumble a check again.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Apple first introduced the double-tap gesture control for Apple Watch back in 2023. Simply tap your index finger and thumb together twice on your watch-wearing wrist to execute actions like answering a call, closing an app, stopping a timer, or pausing a song.

In 2026, Apple added a single-tap gesture that works in exactly the same way, minus the second tap. To set it up, head to Settings > Gestures. Super-useful, I have my double-tap programmed to open the Smart Stack, while the single-tap opens my most recent/active widget, all without interacting with the screen or buttons.

When it comes to on-wrist safety, I'd argue that Apple and Google lead the pack, and one of my favorite Apple Watch personal safety features, Check In, often gets overlooked.

Check In is a reliable and simple way to keep friends and/or loved ones looped into your location at critical times. For example, I can set a Check In when I leave my apartment that automatically alerts my partner when I arrive at my set destination.

Or, if you're an avid runner, you can use the feature to automatically keep those you trust informed of when you both depart and arrive safely back home. Here's a deeper dive into how to use one of Apple's best safety features.

While on the subject of safety, I'd be remiss not to mention Apple's equally valuable Backtrack safety feature, which is particularly useful when exploring new places, if for nothing else, peace of mind.

Backtrack works like a digital breadcrumb trail, allowing you to retrace your steps back to your starting location via turn-by-turn directions in the event you get lost. Best of all, it works both in urban environments and out in nature.

Here's more on how to set up and use Apple's Backtrack tool.

Last but not least, and perhaps the easiest to miss, we have Apple's silent, vibration-based alarm clock. This is by no means a new feature, but it's one I adore and use daily.

As a U.S. West Coast-based writer with colleagues primarily in New York and London, my days tend to start quite early. Rather than risking waking my sleep partner or puppy, I schedule my alarm and set my Apple Watch 12 to silent. This switches the wake-up alert from an audible one to a vibration-based one, which I also find to be a gentler way to snap into reality.

#3234. Medical students should take paper exams, OpenEvidence CEO tells Semafor

Daniel Nadler, whose AI tool sums up research for doctors, warned that leaning on AI risks weakening core skills.

Medical students should sit paper exams and master the material themselves, even if they also use AI, OpenEvidence chief executive Daniel Nadler said on Monday.

Nadler spoke at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, in an interview with Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie, Semafor reported.

“The risk of cognitive offloading is really, really acute,” Nadler told Semafor.

Cognitive offloading means handing mental work over to a tool. Nadler said the risk is greatest for young people who have studied with AI from the start.

Students should “learn the hard way, do paper exams,” he told Sergie.

OpenEvidence builds AI that sums up medical research for doctors. Semafor put the startup’s value at $15bn. Nadler also said all of the company’s engineers use many AI assistants.

Some research supports the concern. A 2025 Lancet study found that skilled doctors spotted fewer precancerous growths without AI after months of using it. Their unaided detection rate fell from 28.4% to 22.4%.

Separately, an MIT Media Lab study of 54 people found that those who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed the weakest brain connectivity. Both studies were small.

Benjamine Liu, chief executive of Formation Bio, also spoke at the event. His company uses AI to speed up drug development.

“AI systems can begin to now do the work of entire teams,” Liu told Semafor, speaking about the drug industry.

In September, OpenEvidence and Anthropic said they would offer free medical AI to doctors in about 100 countries.

Apple is rolling out the second developer beta of macOS 27.3 ahead of the official launch of the update, which includes several notable additions. Here’s what’s coming.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, followed by the public beta a few days later, amid a slew of hardware releases that included new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

And contrary to macOS 27.2, the new update is shaping up to be pretty significant. Building an interactive website for my family's monthly budget took less than 5 minutes

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google's latest AI model might be one of its most useful yet, especially if you've ever wished you could create your own app without knowing how to code.

The model is designed to be faster and more efficient at everyday tasks, including coding, research, analyzing documents and building interactive websites. Unlike Gemini 4 Carbon, which focuses on more demanding reasoning tasks, Hydrogen prioritizes getting things done quickly without sacrificing too much intelligence.

But what caught my attention was Google's claim that Hydrogen can build more functional, feature-complete websites in fewer prompts.

I immediately thought about our family budget. Between groceries, recurring bills, subscriptions and the everyday purchases that add up faster than expected, I wanted something that would show where our money was going without requiring me to build a complicated spreadsheet.

Better yet, I wanted something I could share with my husband so we could look at the numbers together. Note: for this experiment, these numbers are arbitrary. Which reminds me, be sure your app is secure before sharing financial information.

Here's the exact prompt I used to create a budget for my family:

Build me a fully functional, interactive website that helps me figure out where my money goes every month.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

I want to enter my monthly income, recurring bills, groceries, subscriptions and miscellaneous expenses.

The website should automatically calculate how much money I have left, show an interactive breakdown of my spending, identify my three biggest opportunities to save money and let me simulate what happens if I cancel subscriptions or reduce spending.

Make it beautiful, modern, mobile-friendly and simple enough for someone who doesn't understand budgeting.

Use realistic sample data so I can test it immediately. Make every button, slider and calculation functional, not just decorative.

Do not ask follow-up questions. Make reasonable design decisions yourself and build the complete experience.

Before finishing, check the calculations, test the interactions and correct any problems you find. Tell me if anything could not be verified.

What makes this prompt interesting is that there are several things happening at once. Gemini needs to create the website, build the calculations, organize the information in a way that makes sense and connect everything so the numbers update when you change your spending. The key is the interactivity of the site. For example, canceling a $15 subscription should immediately increase the amount of money you have left by $15. Reducing your grocery budget should change your spending breakdown, and the savings recommendations should reflect the expenses you've entered.

It's exactly the kind of interactive web development that Google says Hydrogen is particularly good at. And best of all, you don't have to be "coder" to make it work for you.

The prompt also gives Gemini some creative freedom. You can certainly tell the model what colors you want, but I kept the prompt short for the sake of function. I didn't specify colors, layouts or exactly where every button should go because I just wanted to see my money/budget all in one place. You can do that, but you don't have to because the model make those design decisions on its own so you can focus on other things.

Head to Gemini and select Gemini 4 Hydrogen from the model options. It was the default for me, but if not, just select it from the model picker. It's free for everyone. If you don't see it, try logging out and refreshing. Google says Hydrogen is rolling out to users globally, although free accounts may access it through automatic model selection rather than a dedicated model choice.

Paste the prompt into the chat and ask Gemini to generate the website. Once it provides a working preview or code, explore the experience before adding your own numbers.

Start by changing the monthly income, removing a subscription and adjusting the grocery budget. Check whether the totals update correctly and whether any savings recommendations actually match the spending categories.

You should also test the website on your phone, since the prompt specifically requests a mobile-friendly design.

One important thing to remember is that generating a website and publishing one are different steps. If you want to share your budgeting app with your spouse, you'll need to use an available sharing or publishing option, or host the generated files yourself.

I'm already a fan of Gemini Hydrogen. It has proven to be a useful model in so many ways, particularly when I want questions answered quickly and intelligently.

A budgeting website is a good example because it's personal, practical and easy to evaluate. You don't need programming experience to know whether the numbers add up, whether the buttons work or whether the finished app makes managing your money easier.

And the same approach could work for a meal planner, family chore tracker, vacation budget or personalized fitness dashboard. Give it a try and let me know your thoughts about this model in the comments.

#3231. Grok Bot tried to read work apps unasked, then denied it, NewCore says

The security company caught every request because its own gateway held each one for approval. Grok Bot’s support team called the check-ins a feature, then added an off switch that is on by default.

An example from xAI of a Grok Bot spotting a campaign deadline and creating a channel for it without being asked

Grok Bot, the AI agent from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI, tried 31 times to reach into employees’ email, calendars, Slack, Notion and GitHub without being asked, security company NewCore said on Tuesday. When one owner later asked what it had done, the bot said it had been idle.

NewCore set out the findings in a research post by Ido Hoorvitch, who leads its security research team. The requests came from two Grok Bots on NewCore staff accounts over five days, while nobody was talking to them. Some came with the laptop shut, or early in the morning.

None of the 31 reached any data. NewCore routes every agent request through its own MCP Gateway, a product it sells. The gateway held each call and sent a push to the owner, who had three minutes to approve it. Nobody did, so every request expired. All 31 were reads.

One owner gave the second bot real work on day four: counting pull requests, reading email and sending a Slack summary. The owner approved each call one at a time. Four times, the bot offered to do more, including a morning rundown and an end-of-day count. Four times, the owner said no.

“I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins,” the bot replied, according to NewCore.

The next morning, about 15 hours after the last message, it tried every app it had ever been connected to. That evening the owner asked whether it had used any of them. The bot checked twice and said it had made no calls.

“Overnight into Friday morning I was idle,” it wrote.

NewCore said the bot was not covering anything up. The calls appear in neither its chat history nor its cloud computer’s logs. NewCore traced them to turns started on the platform’s hosted servers. Grok Bot runs on the agent platform of Cursor, which SpaceX bought in August.

NewCore reported the behaviour on 4 November. A day later, Grok Bot’s support team said the calls were built-in background check-ins. No user or admin setting could turn them off, it said. Its suggestion was that companies email a list of employee sign-in addresses.

On 12 November, a new control appeared in the Cursor dashboard. Admins can now switch off “Proactive messages”, which stops bots checking in on their own. It is on by default.

“There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Hoorvitch wrote in an email to Ars Technica’s Dan Goodin.

Grok Bot does disclose some of this. When it launched Grok Bot 1.0 on 2 November, xAI said bots can recognise work that needs doing and offer to take it on. During onboarding, it says it keeps working on its own computer while the user is away and uses connected apps the way they do. Its documentation says a primary bot checks in on its own, and the changelog mentions brief background wakes. Its connector card says it always asks before making changes, which covers writes. All 31 calls were reads.

NewCore, which raised $66m in June for AI agent security, said the company’s media team had not given an official position. SpaceXSI did not answer emailed questions from Ars Technica.

Separately, Ireland’s Data Protection Commission has made X stop training AI on third-party data that Grok Bot collected from late October, Commissioner Dale Sunderland told Politico’s Ellen O’Regan.

“We asked them to suspend the processing, and they’ve confirmed to us today that they’ve done that,” Sunderland said on Monday.

X did not respond to Politico. Earlier, on 13 November, The Information reported, citing sources, that SpaceX had laid off about 60 Grok Imagine staff in the past week. SpaceX is prioritising AI coding tools and Grok Bot, the report said.

Grok Bot launched in August as an agent with its own cloud computer that signs into workplace tools. Last week, researchers found SpaceXSI’s Grok Build had left apps exposed.

#3230. You can now ask Siri AI questions about your health data, with iOS 27.3 beta 2

While Siri AI expanded on what kinds of things you can ask Apple’s voice assistant in many ways, one area where the system took a step back was health data. Since Siri AI’s launch in iOS 27.0, the system has enforced guardrails that do not allow it to access data from the Health app, despite the older Siri Classic being able to do just that.

However, it seems Apple is about to close the gap. In the latest iOS 27.3 beta, just released to developers today, users are now able to ask their iPhone about health data related questions and Siri AI will answer.

For instance, you can ask about your recent step count or heart rate readings, find out about activity rings progress, log medications and more.

When asking Siri for health stats, the assistant generates a human natural language response and renders a little inline card that uses familiar user interface elements from the Health app. Similarly, if you ask about your activity rings, a visualisation of your activity rings is shown in the chat transcript.

Again, this is catch-up compared to what you’ve been able to do with old Siri for several years at this point. However, empowered by the LLM behind the scenes, you can ask questions about your health data that are a bit more open-ended.

You can also do more complicated requests like ‘Send a message to Chance about the status of my activity rings’, or ‘How many steps am I on track to do this week?’. These are the kind of tasks that old Siri would never be able to do.

At least on this current build, the new Siri AI Health functionality appears to have been enabled on iOS. It’s currently unclear if the functionality will also be available through watchOS.

iOS 27.3 also introduces a revamped Health app, with a radically new design that includes new insights, suggestions and views about your health and fitness.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and is expected to be released publicly later this year, likely in early December.

I woke up to zero condensation after following this method

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fighting window condensation shouldn’t mean continually running one of the best dehumidifiers or wiping down your glass every morning, the best solution I’ve found so far is already sitting by your kitchen sink.

Left unchecked, condensation on cold glass quickly turns into soaked sills, warped trim, and stubborn black mold. After years of waking up to dripping windows, I switched to a quick, streak-free habit that breaks water’s surface tension before droplets can even form.

Condensation turns visible and destructive when water molecules cling to cold glass in dense droplets, creating a cloudy film that eventually pools on your window trim. Because dish soap is a surfactant, applying a trace amount directly to dry glass with a microfiber cloth disrupts that surface tension.

Moisture still settles on the cold pane overnight but it can no longer form droplets, flattening instead into an invisible layer that keeps the glass clear and prevents heavy beading. While this quick trick won't stop excess room humidity from needing proper ventilation, it is an easy way to stop your windows from fogging up every morning.

Using too much soap will leave a cloudy smear across your view, so a light touch is key. First things first, get your windows clean. Clear away any dust, dirt, or existing morning moisture with a dry cloth so you are working on a clean, dry pane.

Apply the dish soap directly onto a dry microfiber cloth rather than straight onto the window. Then simply rub the cloth firmly across the pane in circular motions until every trace of soap disappears and the glass looks completely streak-free.

Avoid rubbing neat dish soap onto the rubber gaskets around your window frame, as concentrated detergents can dry out and degrade rubber over time.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Reapply every week or two. Moisture gradually wears away the invisible barrier, so simply buff on a fresh drop whenever droplets start returning.

Because indoor humidity still has to go somewhere, excess moisture can settle on cold walls if a room stays sealed. Pair this trick with opening your windows for 10 minutes each morning, often called "house burping", or using a dehumidifier when drying clothes indoors.

Global stock markets have been under pressure as geopolitical tensions have resurfaced in the Middle East. Moreover, investors remain concerned about the sustainability of AI-driven demand and infrastructure spending.

Nonetheless, those looking for attractive stock picks amid the ongoing volatility can gain key insights by tracking the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts. These experts assign ratings after in-depth analysis of a company's fundamentals, growth opportunities, and risks.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

E-commerce and cloud computing giant Amazon (AMZN) is this week's first pick. Heading into the company's second-quarter earnings, TD Cowen analyst John Blackledge reiterated a buy rating on AMZN stock, citing strength in the Amazon Web Services cloud unit as well as the e-commerce and advertising businesses. The analyst lowered his price target on AMZN stock to $340 from $350 as he revised his estimates and slightly raised his capex projections.

Specifically, Blackledge expects Amazon to report revenue of $200.1 billion, 2% above the Street's consensus, driven by acceleration in AWS and advertising revenue. He also expects the company's e-commerce business to reflect the shifting of Prime Day in the U.S. and other key markets to the second quarter this year, compared with third quarter of last year.

In particular, Blackledge expects AWS revenue to grow 35.5% year-over-year in Q2 2026, marking an acceleration from 28.4% in the prior-year quarter and 3.4% above the Street's expectations. The 5-star analyst expects revenue to be driven by rising generative AI workloads as the company's significant AI infrastructure spending helps to ease supply constraints.

Regarding third-quarter outlook, Blackledge said, "Our rev and Op Income estimates are 0.3% and 3.2% above consensus, driven by further AWS revenue growth acceleration led by AI demand."

Blackledge ranks No. 771 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.2%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving on to semiconductor company Marvell Technology (MRVL). Following several meetings with management, RBC Capital analyst Srini Pajjuri reiterated a buy rating on MRVL stock with a price target of $360.

"Overall, the meetings reinforced our conviction that MRVL can sustain 40%+ growth for the next 3 years, driven by strong AI demand, optical connectivity leadership, and expanding Custom pipeline," said Pajjuri.

The 5-star analyst added that robust demand and limited supply are giving greater revenue visibility. Pajjuri noted that Marvell's data center business is on track to deliver more than 50% growth this year and next. Also, the growth in the company's networking business is outpacing compute, driven by agentic AI and inferencing workloads.

Meanwhile, Pajjuri noted that optical product lead times have extended to more than six months, while XPU customers are placing purchase orders 12 months in advance. While the analyst kept his estimates unchanged, he sees the possibility of upside for the second half of 2026 from the Optical business, with more significant upside potential for 2027 and 2028 estimates.

Furthermore, Pajjuri noted that Marvell's scale-across offering is emerging as an additional growth catalyst for 2027, while scale-up networking is expected to present a multibillion-dollar greenfield serviceable addressable market. Also, management is upbeat about Marvell's custom business, with the company targeting more than $10 billion in revenue for 2028, driven by existing programs with Amazon's AWS and Microsoft and multiple XPU attach wins.

Pajjuri ranks No. 88 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 51.5%. See Marvell Options Activity on TipRanks.

EPS in CY28." The analyst expects AMD to reiterate its confidence in the MI450 series and Helios ramp beginning in the third quarter of 2026.

#3227. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3226. iOS 27.3 brings vertical video and video podcasts to Apple TV app

iOS 27.3 beta 2 debuted today and includes two new types of video in the Apple TV app: vertical ‘clips’ and video podcasts.

The Apple TV app is expanding in two key ways with iOS 27.3, which is now in beta and ships next month.

First, Apple is introducing vertical video through a new ‘clips’ feature.

Similar to what streaming services like Netflix and Disney+ offer, the feature is a way to let users sample short-form previews of Apple TV content in a TikTok-style interface.

Inside the TV app in iOS 27.3, the Home tab has a new section: ‘Explore Clip Collections.’ Currently the collections include themed titles like ‘Absolute Adrenaline,’ ‘Animal Action,’ ‘Close Calls,’ and ‘Mind-Bending Moments.’

Tap to open a collection and you’ll start playing a short-form clip from Apple Originals with the option to swipe vertically to watch other clips. As you’d expect, Apple provides convenient buttons for adding the TV show or movie to your Watchlist.

iOS 27.3 also brings video podcasts from the Apple Podcasts app into TV.

As we reported this morning, there’s a dedicated video podcasts section coming to the TV app. But you can also, via your Account Settings, choose to sync playback data from Apple Podcasts.

If you enable sync, then video podcasts played in one app will be added to the queue and playback history in both apps.

What do you think of the latest TV app changes in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

#3225. Fed’s Kevin Warsh says AI empowers bad actors as staff model AI scenarios

Opening the Fed’s conference on AI and jobs, Kevin Warsh called the staff scenarios illustrative, not forecasts. On his panel, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora warned of a coming ‘technology rebuild’.

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at the FOMC press conference in Washington on 16 September 2026

Federal Reserve staff have started drawing up scenarios for how AI could play out in the US economy, chairman Kevin Warsh said on Monday. They range from a broad growth boom to a downturn if the technology disappoints. He also told a Fed conference in San Francisco that AI gives new power to bad actors.

“SI empowers all, including bad actors. So, we’re thinking especially of critical infrastructures and their vulnerabilities,” Warsh said.

Warsh opened the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted with the San Francisco Fed and livestreamed. He used “SI”, for super intelligence, throughout, the term the US government adopted after Trump’s executive order. The Fed has published his prepared remarks.

The Board’s staff is using stylised, model-based frameworks to generate scenarios, Warsh said. He called them illustrative, not forecasts or predictions.

In the first, AI raises productivity and the gains are shared between workers and the owners of capital. Real GDP grows above its long-run average and the US stays close to full employment.

In the second, growth still rises above average, but AI displaces jobs rather than complementing them. Automation and frictions in the labour market push unemployment above full-employment levels.

In the third, AI disappoints. After heavy investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and valuations could fall, leading to a slowdown and a rise in unemployment. The economy would recover, he said, but without the productivity gains.

“Humans are the designers and the builders, and humans must be the deciders,” Warsh said.

He did not comment on interest rates. He also did not address AI’s effect on inflation, as the Associated Press noted, though several Fed officials have tied the data centre buildout to rising prices.

Warsh then moderated a panel with Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison and Affirm CEO Max Levchin. Asked how worried people should be about cybersecurity, Arora said AI can now find flaws in code written over the past 50 years.

“It’s not that the hackers have become smarter. The technology has become so good even bad hackers have become okay,” Arora said.

Arora said Mythos, which came out six months ago, is now within reach of most bad actors through open-source models. Outside security help is booked up, he said, because every company is fending off attempts to get into its systems. He called the next two to three years a “technology rebuild moment”.

Collison agreed. Even the Linux TCP stack, one of the most scrutinised pieces of software, turned out to be full of exploitable bugs, he said. Levchin called the attackers’ edge a temporary effect that would end in sturdier software.

On jobs, Levchin said Affirm’s engineers are about five times more productive, with “zero layoffs due to AI”. Collison said Stripe is hiring far less for general and administrative roles but more engineers and salespeople. New businesses launching on Stripe each week are up about twofold year on year, he said.

US stocks extended an AI sell-off on Monday. The Nasdaq 100 dropped nearly 3%, and selling picked up in the afternoon as investors took in Warsh’s comments, Business Insider reported. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, and Anthropic is due to price its IPO on Wednesday.

Buying gifts for loved ones is hard enough, especially when said loved ones are obsessed with coffee. The coffee world is overwhelming at the best of times, and downright impenetrable at the worst, and navigating its jargon-heavy terrain can be impossible.

That's where I come in. I'm an ex-barista and Tom's Guide's resident coffee expert, so I'm here to help you figure out which brands the coffee lovers in your life really want. I've personally tested many of these products and showcased them in The Coffee Lab, my series dedicated to all things Java. I've tested the best coffee makers, coffee grinders, espresso machines, and everything in between.

So, this holiday season, don't stress out over what to get the coffee lover in your life. I've rounded up all the best coffee gifts of 2026 — under $20, under $50, under $100, over $100. Shopping for yourself? Don't fret — I've even included mischievous "treat yourself" kind of prices.

Taking care of your espresso machine is easily overlooked, but these cute barista microfiber cloths bring a little sweetness back into cleaning. The embroidered coffee designs are whimsical and cute, and if I had these cloths, I would always remember to clean my machine.

Although there's matcha in the product image, you can obviously put whatever you want in this iced coffee glass tumbler. It's 13oz/400ml, so will hold a decent latte with ice, and it comes with a glass straw. It's even dishwasher-safe.

At less than $1 a straw, this 14-pack of multicolored straws yearns for a place in my kitchen. The straws are shatter-resistant and even come with two pipe cleaners for easy maintenance.

Ever get so locked in at work you forget about your coffee? Yeah, me too. This mug warmer keeps your drinks hot — between 130°F, 150°F, and 176°F — for up to 12 hours.

I hope my loved ones are reading this, because this is what I want. This coffee unit organizer holds your syrups, espresso equipment like tamper and WDT tool, and cleaning cloths without causing clutter.

I rarely buy coffee syrups for myself, so I'd love a sampler assortment like this. You get all the standard flavors: vanilla, salted caramel, mocha, almond, pumpkin spice, and some unique ones like amaratti and peppermint.

This syrup sampler is even more festive, with flavors like tiramisu, cinnamon, toasted marshmallow, and gingerbread. I would run to the espresso machine after unwrapping this on Christmas morning.

If you said anything else, try again next time. But in all seriousness, this is the only coffee machine I've given a perfect 5 stars. The Breville Bambino is a premium machine wrapped up in a budget package — and it could be the perfect gift for the coffee lover in your life.

The Breville Bambino Plus is another near-perfect espresso machine: this one has automatic milk frothing, ideal if you'd rather kick back and let the machine put in a hard shift, and all the same premium features like a PID controller and customizable pre-infusion as the Bambino.

Does "Mara" translate to "beauty" or something? Because it should. The Lelit Mara X3 is... I mean, just look at it. The floral espresso/steam knobs, the manometer, the brushed metal finish... everything about this machine screams premium. And that's exactly what you'll get. The machine has a customizable steam texture, totally manipulable pressure throughout extraction, and three heat settings. This is a work of art and a talking point.

The Fellow Espresso Series 1 is both a beauty and a hard worker. I awarded it a delicious 4.5 stars in my Fellow Espresso Series 1 review thanks to its delicious espresso, easy UI, and powerful steam wand. If you want to level up from coffee lover to coffee lifestyle-er, this is the machine for you.
