#3191. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3189. I tested the Netgear Nighthawk RS150 and this affordable Wi-Fi 7 router delivers plenty of bang for your buck

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It may not be the fastest or have the most features, but budget Wi-Fi 7 routing is the name of the game with Netgear’s Nighthawk RS150.

Add-on Armor security with device scanning

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Wi-Fi Spec: BE5000 (802.11be)Number of Antennas/Removable: 3/NoPorts: One 2.5 Gbps WAN, three 1 Gbps LANProcessor/Memory/Storage: Quad-core 2.0 GHz/1GB/512MBWi-Fi chip: Broadcom BCM6766Peak 802.11ac performance: 1.437 Gbps (at 15 feet)Range: 115 feetSize: 9.8 x 5.9 x 4.0 inchesEstimated Annual Electricity Cost: $13.80

As Wi-Fi 7 routers take over as the spec of choice, Netgear reduces the entry point for creating a competent up to date home network to $180 with its Nighthawk RS150. It may not be the fastest, nor does it cover all three Wi-Fi 7 transmission bands but the RS150 provides speedy data service at a budget price. Its dual-band approach to wireless data hits the spec’s hot buttons except for 6 GHz transmissions and the ultra-wide 320MHz data channels that come with it.

At less than $200, is this the best Wi-Fi router or even the best Wi-Fi 7 router for you? Find out in my full review.

With a list price of $200, the Netgear Nighthawk RS150 tempers performance with price. It can be found online for $180. By contrast, the 2025 Editor’s Choice winner, the TP-Link Archer BE3600, is similar in scope at $120.

The lower output BE3600 Nighthawk RS90 can be had for closer to $100 if you’re on a tight budget but still need to upgrade your Wi-Fi.

Looking a lot like the rest of the Nighthawk RS family, the RS150 has an octagonal tower design. At 9.8 x 5.9 x 4.0 inches, it’s three times as big as the TP-Link Archer BE3600, although it takes up only half of its desktop space.

Inside, the RS150 has three antennas and a Broadcom BCM6766 for 2x2 data movement for the 2.4 GHz band and 3x3 for the 5.0 GHz band. It relies on many of Wi-Fi 7’s tricks to move more data, including 4K Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (QAM). It does without Multi-Link Operations (MLO) and use of Wi-Fi 7’s 6 GHz band and the associated 320MHz data channels, though.

The router’s quad-core 2.0 GHz processor, 1GB of memory and 512MB create a mid-range home LAN to theoretically move up to 700 Mbps over the 2.4 GHz band as well as 4.3 Gbps on the 5.0 GHz band for a BE5000 rating. It falls short of the best with a 2.5 Gbps WAN input and three 1 Gbps LAN ports versus 5 or 10 Gbps inputs and higher-speed downstream connections.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Most will never miss the fourth networking port but if you need it, the best approach is adding a network switch. It does without the Archer BE3600’s USB port for connecting a data drive too.

Up front, the router’s LEDs show the RS150 status for power, Internet, action on its two bands and three wired connections. There’s also a light for using Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and, happily, a button for turning off the lights.

Unlike many of its Wi-Fi 7 brethren, the RS150 runs cool. Its passive cooling scheme pulls room air into the device with warm air exiting the top vents. Even when running hard, the RS150 never got above 87.2 degrees Fahrenheit compared to 20 degrees hotter for its competitors.

The router includes a 30-day trial for Netgear Armor comprehensive security software that uses Bitdefender software and services. After that, you need to pay. It includes virus scanning for a variety of connected devices along with Dark Web monitoring and heightened analysis of the data flow for malicious sites and unauthorized entry.

The standard plan costs $100 a year along with an extension of the product’s one year warranty to three years with service and support; without it the personalized service ends at 90 days.

There’s also the $150 Armor Plus plan that adds Bitdefender’s Virtual Private Network (VPN) in a variety of protocols, including WireGuard and OpenVPN. The subscription also includes anti-tracking and ad blocking.

Based on testing over several weeks of daily use with Keysight’s IxChariot networking benchmark set to mimic 10 high-performance users and an HP Envy x360 test notebook, the RS150 started out strong. Able to connect at 1.467 Gbps with the test system next to the RS150, it offers 15% higher throughput compared to the TP-Link Archer BE3600’s 1.234 Gbps.

Later, with a 15 foot length of Cat 7 cable connecting the two, the network provided 1.527 Gbps. That’s a big step up from the Archer BE3600’s 1.103 Gbps.

It did just as well at real-world wireless distances, starting at 15 feet, where the RS150 moved 1.437 Gbps. This is a nice upgrade over the Archer BE3600’s 1.138 Gbps but well short of the Nighthawk RS700 at 1.773 Gbps or the TP-Link Archer BE9700 at 2.201 Gbps, both of which use all three Wi-Fi transmission bands.

Its mid-range figures fluctuated but ended up at an impressive average of 1.057 Gbps at 50 feet. This scatter might feel like extra latency when the router is stressed but the test system never dropped a connection. Still, it’s a large speed boost over the Archer BE9700 (at 700.7 Mbps), Nighthawk RS700 (691.8 Mbps) or Archer BE3600 (702.3 Mbps).

At 75 feet, the throughput fell to 440.8 Mbps, double that of the Archer BE3600, but, again, with lots of variation. The router had a range of 115 feet and delivered 44.7 Mbps at 90 feet – nearly three times the data flow of the Archer BE3600 at the same distance.

At 1.259 Gbps, the RS150 did well on the wall penetration test where the signal travels across a 20 foot room and then through a wall. That’s just ahead of the Archer BE3600’s 1.114 Gbps.

Over three weeks of daily use, the RS150 proved to be an online home body with the ability to move emails, serve up video and serve up online games. Along the way, it used 9.0 watts as it lacks a power-saving idle mode. If it runs 24/7 and you pay the national average of 17.5 cents per kilowatt hour of electricity, the router might cost $13.80 over the year. That’s a couple dollars a year more than the Archer BE3600’s $11.80 annual electricity estimate.

I used the Nighthawk app to get the RS150 online, starting with installing the Nighthawk app on my Samsung Galaxy S25 phone. I snapped the router’s QR code, added my own network name and password and admin credentials. Then I needed to answer two challenge questions and verify my email.

The router connected on the first try and took a little over 11 minutes to set up.

To personalize the RS150, I started with the Nighthawk app updating the system’s firmware.

Later I used the Device Manager to see who was online, the Internet Speed to check my connection and WiFi Analytics to check on the connection’s signal strength. There are settings for changing the Wi-Fi details and using the guest LAN.

The router’s Traffic Meter shows daily, weekly and monthly data use. Unfortunately, the app squeezes this data into a portrait mode page and does not spread it out in landscape orientation.

I also tapped into the router’s interface with a web browser with a functional yet basic page that has a scrolling ticker for the network names and passwords. In other words, don’t let just anyone see it.

The Advanced pages range from running the hardware as an access point to turning off the LED lights.

As Wi-Fi 7 matures and the gear to enable it comes down in price, Netgear’s Nighthawk RS150 hits a sweet spot with a nice price and superior performance compared to other budget routers. It excels at mid-range distances and range where competitors can’t keep up.

Sure, there’re compromises, like the lack of 6GHz data transmissions, presence of only three downstream wired networking ports and having to pay for personalized support for more than three months. That said, those items pale in comparison to the RS150’s ability to move data around the house and at a peak of over 1.4 Gbps and stay online at 115 feet.

In other words, the Nighthawk RS150 should satisfy most home networkers with performance that’s hard to beat at $180.

#3188. Former Apple chairman Arthur Levinson files to sell $31.8 million in company stock

Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the company.

Today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his plans to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he currently holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

The filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

#3187. Understand How Satellite Links Shape IoT Device Design and Testing

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#3184. iPhone Duo gets one of Face ID’s best features with upcoming iOS 27.3 update

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the new face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

After updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

#3183. The New York Stock Exchange Will Soon Use Avalanche for Tokenized Stocks. Is the Coin a Screaming Buy Right Now?

This is one instance where the details matter more than the headline.

In what might be its biggest news in years, Ava Labs, the company that builds the blockchain behind the cryptocurrency Avalanche (AVAX +1.49%), just said on Nov. 9 that it struck a deal with the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) to be the backend infrastructure for settling tokenized stocks on a new 24/7 alternative trading system (ATS), a venue that matches buyers and sellers of securities without registering as a full stock exchange. If the collaboration delivers everything that holders are hoping for, it could well become the spark of a multiyear comeback arc.

The price of Avalanche is still 95% below its all-time high set in 2021, which could lead some investors to imagine that the coin is still a bargain given this development. So is it a screaming buy right now?

The NYSE's parent company, Intercontinental Exchange (ICE -1.26%), initially announced the new venue back on Jan. 19, describing it as an exchange with 24/7 access to U.S. stocks, instant transaction settlement, and other features like stablecoin-based funding. It's slated to launch in the fourth quarter of this year, pending regulatory approval.

The NYSE said that in its search for a blockchain partner to provide the ledger that clears and settles the exchange's transactions, it wanted a network with predictable transaction costs that could also gate which actors are allowed to participate. The NYSE will run its own custom blockchain built with Avalanche's technology rather than send its transactions over Avalanche's public blockchain network. Those custom networks can charge fees in any token their operator picks. In this case, each network pays 1.33 AVAX coins monthly per computer that verifies transactions (validators), and then the network permanently destroys those coins.

The trouble is that such a small fee is practically irrelevant to Avalanche.

Assuming, purely for illustration, that the NYSE chain ran 20 validators, it would burn about 319.2 AVAX per year, which would be worth about $2,289 at the Nov. 16 price. In the 24-hour period ended at noon on Nov. 16, Avalanche's public network collected $17,605 in transaction fees, more than that hypothetical year of burn.

There's no reason to expect that many thousands of validators would ever be needed. Therefore the direct impact of the fee burns from the exchange's activity on the coin's price is almost guaranteed to be minimal.

The bull case for buying Avalanche right now is thus fairly indirect.

The NYSE chain could in theory connect to Avalanche's wider ecosystem, which in turn could push some activity onto the public blockchain. Beyond the small validator fees, that's the main way the deal could reach coin holders.

Scale is the other unknown. ICE describes the platform as a new venue, so it may handle only a sliver of the NYSE's business. It's also faintly possible that it could handle a large helping of that business.

Nonetheless, landing the NYSE as a customer could help Avalanche to get more financial institutions interested in its network. During the next few quarters, watch how much activity there is when the platform launches and whether Avalanche or ICE allows AVAX any real role in fees or even staking on the NYSE chain.

If neither happens by mid-2027, this coin is probably not something that is worth buying -- which is the same as the present state of affairs.

#3180. Rocket Lab Says Adjusted EBITDA Turns Positive Within 6 Months of Neutron’s First Flight. Here’s the Date That Implies.

The space services company plans to launch its Neutron rocket next year.

Rocket Lab(RKLB -1.60%), a developer of reusable orbital rockets and other spacecraft components, has successfully launched its Electron rocket 99 times to date. But its second rocket, the larger Neutron, has been repeatedly delayed since its introduction in 2021.

Rocket Lab originally planned to launch the Neutron in 2024, but it eventually pushed that target back to 2025 and 2026. But in October, it postponed the Neutron's first launch again to 2027.

Those setbacks were discouraging, since the Neutron would have helped Rocket Lab compete more effectively against SpaceX's (SPCX +2.32%) Falcon 9 rockets. But during Rocket Lab's third-quarter conference call on Nov. 11, CFO Adam Spice claimed the company's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) would turn positive within roughly six months of Neutron's first successful test flight.

Rocket Lab believes that will happen as Neutron's launch removes the rocket's heavy development expenses from its bottom line. It also expects the Neutron to unlock a much larger, higher-margin commercial market for its Launch Services segment.

Assuming that it can achieve those goals, analysts expect Rocket Lab's adjusted EBITDA to come in at positive $41 million in 2027 -- compared to negative $55 million in 2026. So while Rocket Lab hasn't given us a clear date for its first Neutron launch yet, we can optimistically assume it will happen sometime within the first half of 2027 to hit Wall Street's targets.

#3178. Face unlock is a good compromise for the iPhone Duo – now let’s have it for the Mac

When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security …

The first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Meantime, in 2017 Apple launched Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple said at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the company is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Currently, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook users have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

What’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

#3177. Jamie Dimon Declared the U.S. Will Hang On to Its Status as the World's Top Reserve Currency. Here's Why That Confidence Matters for Dollar-Denominated Assets JPMorgan Clients Hold.

Jamie Dimon’s not worried about a global loss of confidence in the U.S. dollar.

One big debate in investing right now, and a cause of concern for some economists, is the question: "Will the U.S. dollar keep its status as the world's top reserve currency?" Many Americans who go about their daily business, like shopping for groceries or other household goods, might not think much about this. But it's important.

In the background of everyday life, Americans benefit from a unique privilege: Many countries around the world want to use and hold our currency. The U.S. dollar is the most popular reserve currency for central banks and governments around the world. According to Federal Reserve data, as of 2024, 58.5% of total global foreign exchange reserves were held in U.S. dollars. The euro was in a distant second place, making up about 19%, followed by the Japanese yen at 5.6%.

There's been some debate about whether this will continue. What if the U.S. dollar becomes less popular than other international currencies? What if America has a government debt crisis and investors flee American assets? What if the world loses confidence in America?

Jamie Dimon, the CEO of JPMorgan Chase (JPM -1.15%), made headlines for casting doubt upon those doubts. Dimon believes that the American dollar's status as the global reserve currency is not in danger -- as long as two important U.S. strengths stay in place.

If Dimon is correct, that could be good news for investors in U.S. dollar-denominated assets. Let's look at what the JPMorgan Chase CEO had to say, and why it matters for your investments.

Speaking at the Economic Club of Chicago last month, Dimon expressed confidence in the U.S. dollar and said he doesn't believe it will lose its status as the world's most popular reserve currency. He said that the two most important factors in the U.S. dollar's dominance of foreign reserves are the U.S. military and the overall strength of the U.S. economy.

"If we have the strongest military in the world and the strongest economy in the world, we will be the preeminent reserve currency," Dimon said.

Foreign governments and central banks tend to hold dollars because the dollar is widely used in international trade and is generally considered a safe, stable, and liquid asset. It's easy to move money with U.S. dollars or exchange U.S. Treasury bonds for cash. Not every country offers these advantages. The U.S. dollar's role as the No. 1 reserve currency also reflects America's strengths as a place to invest: a stable government, a strong economy, and the rule of law to protect investors' rights and freedoms.

Dimon's argument is that as long as America's economy leads the world and the U.S. military helps ensure global stability and protects international free trade, America will be a safe and desirable place for investors worldwide to put their money. That's good news for the U.S. dollar and investors in American stocks and bonds.

Since so many banks, investors, and governments around the world trust the dollar and want to buy it, it creates demand that keeps the dollar’s value strong relative to other currencies. It also helps keep U.S. interest rates lower, enabling American consumers, businesses, and the U.S. government to keep borrowing money.

What if that all went away? A June 2026 research paper by Stanford University finance professors found that if the dollar lost its status as a foreign reserve currency, there would be adverse consequences. According to their model, the dollar would depreciate by 8.8%, the U.S. real interest rate would rise by about 0.9%, and there would be an aggregate loss of wealth of about one year of U.S. GDP (about $30.8 trillion, as of 2025).

The good news is that it seems highly unlikely that the U.S. will lose its status as the world's favorite foreign currency -- at least not anytime soon, and not all at once. Other countries' currencies have some disadvantages that make them unlikely to replace the dollar.

If you believe that the U.S. dollar will stay strong, you might want to keep investing in U.S. stocks, such as those in the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -0.39%). The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.40%) is a simple way to buy shares of the 500 largest publicly traded companies in America. If the U.S. economy performs well and the U.S. dollar remains strong, the companies in this S&P 500 ETF will likely benefit in the long term.

#3176. Apple memory suppliers expect price increases through at least 2030 [U]

Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”

Apple said back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

#3173. Major websites compromised to steal crypto from iPhone users

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen …

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Several of the affected companies said that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme says almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly update all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

#3171. Prediction: Nov. 18 Will Be a Big Day for Nvidia for 2 Reasons

Turmoil shook Nvidia and its shareholders last week.

Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%), once a market sensation, has been the subject of turmoil in recent days. Chief executive officer Jensen Huang stepped down following allegations of two affairs, leaving investors with many questions about the company's next moves and overall strategy.

Prior to the current troubles, Nvidia delivered quarter after quarter of earnings growth, with revenue and profit reaching record levels in the billions of dollars. As a result, the stock soared too, climbing 1,100% over the past three calendar years.

Now, I predict that Nov. 18 will be a big day for Nvidia and its shareholders for two reasons -- let's check out the key events to watch this week.

First, though, a quick summary of the Nvidia story and current troubles. Nvidia has become almost a household name in recent years thanks to the company's dominance in the AI market. This tech giant sells the most powerful AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), and has innovated on an annual basis to stay ahead of rivals. The company also expanded into a variety of related products and services and struck partnerships and signed deals with key players to broaden its reach.

All of these moves helped Nvidia construct an AI empire. Founder and chief, Jensen Huang, played a major role in this transformation of Nvidia from a seller of chips mainly to video gaming companies to a giant in the AI market. Huang spoke extensively about AI at events around the world and had strong visibility into where the technology was heading next -- this knowledge, along with his relationships with other tech leaders, made Huang a major figure in the AI space, and a leader capable of driving Nvidia's next wave of successes.

Last week, however, allegations of affairs arose; one involved a woman U.S. intelligence is calling a Chinese spy, and the other involved an Nvidia executive. Nvidia's board, which immediately launched an investigation into Huang's relationship with the former, then went on to meet to discuss Nvidia's future. Huang resigned soon afterward, and Nvidia named Colette Kress, who had been chief financial officer, as interim CEO as the search for a permanent leader is conducted.

Meanwhile, Nvidia's stock, which was up about 25% this year through the end of October, is now down 12%. After Huang's resignation, the shares fell about 4% in the trading session. The recent news clearly put pressure on the stock, but investors are also looking at the company's solid technology and customer relationships -- these elements haven't changed.

Now, let's consider the two events that I predict will make Nov. 18 a big day for Nvidia. On Nov. 17, after the closing bell, Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings, and the next morning, Colette Kress is holding a company meeting.

"You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9 a.m." Pacific time, Kress wrote in a staff email obtained by CNBC.

The earnings report and call, as well as the company meeting, may offer investors clues about Nvidia's strategy in the months following Huang's departure. Though investors know Kress well from previous earnings calls, where she's played a big role, this week, she will be in a different position. Investors will get to know Kress as the interim leader of the company. It's important to note that Nvidia's search for a permanent CEO is considering internal and external candidates, so Kress may be on the list.

My prediction is that any significant messages about strategy, what's next for the company, or forecasts for revenue in the coming quarters could offer the stock direction in the following days. The stock's performance so far shows that some investors are worried, but this isn't a sharp and general sentiment; it's clear that other investors are waiting to learn more before making a move.
