#3149. Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

If you're an Ubuntu user considering a leap to Fedora, but you're hesitating, I explain why you should go ahead and just do it.

In the world of Linux, distro hopping is practically a spectator sport. At some point, we get bored with the distro we’re using and decide to try something new. Perhaps there’s a distro that offers better features, works with more hardware, or has a larger support community. There are so many reasons for switching distros.

Also: Ubuntu 26.04 vs. Fedora 44: My verdict

However, for those new to Linux, the idea of leaving behind a distribution that’s been working just fine can be daunting, especially when you’re considering jumping to a distribution that isn’t as familiar and uses different technology.

As a new Linux user decades ago, I started with Caldera Open Linux 1.0 and immediately jumped to Red Hat Linux 5.2 (before Red Hat became Fedora). I stayed with Red Hat for years, until I found Ubuntu (I believe it was version 4).

Back then, making the jump wasn’t nearly as easy as it is now; in fact, it was unnerving. I was so used to how Fedora did things that I wasn’t certain I’d be able to acclimate.

But I did! And then, after realizing that hopping from one distro to another wasn’t the end of the world, I hopped around for a few years, from distro to distro until I settled back on Ubuntu-based distributions.

Also: Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next

It’s a lot, but it doesn’t have to be nearly as daunting as it seems. In fact, it can be exciting and fun. If you’re considering a jump from Ubuntu to Fedora, let me try to ease your concerns.

First, let’s get the obvious out of the way: Ubuntu and Fedora are both Linux. It’s not like you’re jumping from Windows or MacOS to Linux. This is a lateral move, which is not nearly as fear-inducing.

Beyond that, Ubuntu and Fedora are much more similar than you might expect. They both have GUI tools for everything you need; they’re both secure; they both have great package managers and package manager front-ends; they both make it easy to install all of the software you need (and all of the software you need is readily available); and they’re both user-friendly.

Also: 5 of my favorite Linux distros for AI – and why

If you get beyond the GUI and dip your toes into the command line, they both (mostly) use the same commands. Yes, there are some variations, but when you’re first learning the CLI (if you ever do — it’s not necessary), you’ll find those basic commands on Ubuntu are exactly the same as they are on Fedora.

If you migrated from Windows to Ubuntu, you’ve already experienced what a faster operating system feels like. If you jump from Ubuntu to Fedora, you’re going to experience that again, because Fedora is (somewhat) faster than Ubuntu. The difference might not be as exaggerated as it was when you went from Windows to Linux, but it is noticeable. Animations are faster, apps open faster, and switching between desktops is faster — nearly every aspect of Fedora is a bit faster than in Ubuntu.

Also: Fedora 44 made me forget I was using Linux – in the best way

I’ve tested several aspects with regard to the speed of Ubuntu and Fedora, and here are my conclusions:

This is almost a tie. When rebooting from a logged-in desktop to the login screen, Fedora took 13.69 seconds, while Ubuntu took 14.31 seconds. The only caveat to that is if Fedora has updates that require a reboot, in which case Fedora takes considerably longer. The only time you have to reboot Ubuntu after an update is if the kernel is upgraded.

Fedora wins this one, especially when it comes to Flatpak and Snap apps. Snap apps simply cannot compete with the speed of Flatpak apps (more on this in a bit). I tested this by opening a Snap app on Ubuntu and a Flatpak app on Fedora, using GIMP (since I know GIMP takes a while to start). On Fedora, the Flatpak GIMP took 3.48 seconds, and on Ubuntu the Snap app version of GIMP took 4.34 seconds.

This is one area where Ubuntu has a slight edge, but only when installing via the default package manager (rather than Flatpak or Snap). I tested this by timing the installation of Audacity using each package manager (DNF5 and APT) from the command line. DNF5 installed Audacity in 15.34 seconds, whereas the Ubuntu installation took 14.61 seconds.

Generally speaking, Fedora not only ships with newer apps than Ubuntu, but it also gets updates faster than Ubuntu. That’s not to say that Ubuntu uses out-of-date packages; rather, Fedora is more cutting-edge than Ubuntu.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for

At the same time, that doesn’t mean Fedora uses unstable applications. All software that ships and/or is updated on Fedora is well-tested and stable — it’s just fresher.

Flatpaks and Snaps are universal package managers. Fedora ships with Flatpak, and Ubuntu is all-in on Snaps. While these two technologies have the same goal (making software installation easier and more secure), they take different approaches.

First off, Flatpak was created by Red Hat, while Snap was created by Canonical. Snap is partially proprietary, while Flatpak is fully open-source. Flatpak enforces mandatory sandboxing, whereas Snap makes sandboxing optional. Flatpak apps launch faster than Snap apps. Finally, Snap packages are automatically updated, whereas Flatpak apps require manual updates.

Also: My favorite GNOME-based Linux distros

Overall, Flatpak is widely considered the superior technology by the Linux community.

In my experience, Flatpak is a better technology for the desktop, whereas Snap is best suited for servers.

If you were to look at both Ubuntu and Fedora, you would swear they use different desktop environments. Au contraire, mon ami. Both Fedora and Ubuntu use GNOME; the difference is that Ubuntu customizes GNOME to look more like the Ubuntu Unity UI Canonical tested back in 2010. Since then, Ubuntu adopted GNOME and customized it so it wouldn’t irk users who had grown accustomed to Unity.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

Fedora, on the other hand, sticks with a stock installation of GNOME for its flagship release. The good news is that, if you like the Ubuntu take on GNOME, you can install the necessary GNOME extensions (the main one being Dash to Panel) to get a similar layout. You can also get the Unity-like top bar by installing the Unite-Shell extension.

#3148. Apple Launches New App to Study How People Use AI for Health

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Since 2019, when Apple first launched its Research app, the company has partnered with medical universities and institutions to run a range of health studies on hearing, heart health and movement, women’s health and, most recently, the Apple Health Study, which covers a wide variety of health areas.

On Sunday, Apple launched its latest study, and it comes with its own app: the Apple Health AI Study.

During a press briefing, Apple said the study aims to understand how people interact with conversational health AI tools. To do so, it will examine comprehension, response quality, the drivers of user trust and everyday health actions.

The goal? To inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for both Apple and the industry and to explore how health AI might help people prepare for doctor’s visits. Key questions the study aims to address include: Do users understand the information provided by health AI? Do they trust it? Is it helpful?

This is particularly relevant considering that one in three US adults use AI chatbots for health information.

Study data will not be used to train AI models, but it may inform Apple’s feature development.

To facilitate the study, Apple is partnering with OpenEvidence, an AI platform designed specifically for doctors. It generates answers using medical information from these partners: The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, National Comprehensive Cancer Network, Nature and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

In the dedicated app, study participants can ask the AI their text-based health questions and then see answers with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations. They can also choose to share their HealthKit data, including sleep, lab results, activity and resting heart rate, for more personalized answers.

HealthKit is Apple’s hub for health and fitness data collected on the iPhone and Apple Watch.

The Apple Health AI Usage Study is open to 200,000 participants. You must be in the US and age 21 or older to participate. An Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later is also required.

Why an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone? According to Apple, the study app requires the processing capabilities of those iPhones, and it uses on-device Apple Foundation Models that are part of Apple Intelligence. These models provide access to any large language model. For example, as part of the study, these models are used to classify question categories.

Each participant is asked to participate for up to 12 months. During this time, they can ask questions about general health, specific symptoms, recovery from a procedure and their own uploaded health data, as examples.

In addition to a baseline survey, participants will receive monthly surveys and additional surveys specific to preparing for doctor’s visits.

Participants will also be prompted to check in with the app. For instance, if you have a paired Apple Watch, you will receive notifications to check in, along with suggested topics to explore.

If there is a complete lack of participation, a participant may potentially be removed from the study.

After downloading the Apple Health AI Study app, participants must complete a mandatory onboarding process that includes informed consent. They will also be asked to share their demographic information, such as race, age and education level, which will be used to explore how these factors may affect their preferences and communication needs. Then, they can start asking the AI questions.

The iPhone first processes questions using tools designed to remove details that could identify participants. They then go to a secure cloud-based study environment managed by a third-party study support contractor called UST Global, where queries are delinked from individual participant IDs and screened using tools designed to further remove any remaining personal details. Lastly, this info is sent to OpenEvidence, where answers are generated using supporting reference materials.

OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours.

A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types.

Within the study app, there are also safety guardrails that detect concerning questions and respond by suggesting that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed.

There is no live monitoring, and study staff won’t contact participants if any questions related to self-harm are asked.

It’s also up to the participant whether they share any HealthKit metrics. They will first have to choose to upload their clinical health records to Apple’s Health app, and then separately choose to share those records from the Health app to the new Apple Health AI Study app.

The Apple Health AI Study app is now available in the App Store. As of now, there is no set publication date for the study.

Every week, I cast an eye over the latest arrivals on Prime Video, all in an effort to pick out the latest thrillers added to the streaming service library.

While November continues to be dominated by Christmas movies, I've still been able to find three worthwhile thrillers. Okay, so one is more of an action-horror, but it does have its share of thriller-style twists and turns. The other two are a psychological trip and an '80s classic starring Matthew "Ferris Bueller" Broderick. Each one is worthy of your streaming consideration.

So, let's jump into the three new to Prime Video thriller movies I recommend you watch this week.

Perhaps the most “traditional” thriller among my picks this week, “Blink Twice” might not reinvent the genre, but it’s an intense watch that slowly builds tension until a shocking twist. It marked the directorial debut of Zoë Kravitz, and stars Naomi Ackie, most recently seen in “Clayface,” alongside Channing Tatum. It’s an effective first filmmaking effort from Kravitz, even if it’s perhaps not quite as intelligently plotted as the strong first act suggests.

Frida (Naomi Ackie) is a cocktail waitress at a swanky party where she meets tech tycoon Slater King (Channing Tatum). Invited to his private island for a vacation of unparalleled luxury, Frida and her friend Jess (Alia Shawkat) initially think they’ve found paradise, and Frida might have even found love with the charming tech mogul. But as lazy sun-soaked days blur into nights of glamorous partying, Frida can’t shake an uneasy feeling that something is wrong.

Three years before starring in one of the most popular movies of the 1980s, Matthew Broderick made his breakthrough with his second major feature film role. He might have made his debut in “Max Dugan Returns” in the spring of 1983. However, it was the techno-thriller “Wargames” released in the summer that saw Broderick identified as a talent to watch, and, well, those labeling him a rising star at the time were certainly proved right.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Sure, it’s a little outdated in the 21st century, but "Wargames" is still a compelling mix of technology-driven thrills and teen drama. David Lightman (Broderick) is a gifted high schooler but with a lazy streak. A computer whiz, he uses his aptitude for computers to unknowingly access a military central computer with the ability to simulate and even launch a devastating nuclear attack against the USSR. Unaware that he’s playing with real weapons of war and thinking he’s playing a video game, he might have ignited World War III.

Rounding out my picks this week is “They Will Kill You,” a real genre-blender that mixes action, horror, comedy, and thriller elements into a movie that isn’t exactly tonally consistent, but does have quite a few slick moments. Most notably, there's a very fiery action sequence and a satisfying early reveal that flips the storyline on its head. It’s also a great showcase for Zazie Beetz, who is best known for her TV roles in “Atlanta,” “Easy” and “Invincible.”

Asia (Beetz) arrives at a posh New York City high-rise apartment building posing as a maid, but she’s really hoping to find her missing sister. Once in the complex, she discovers it’s not just home to the city's wealthy and elite, but houses a satanic cult. I’ll say no more for fear of spoiling the surprises within this action-horror, but let’s say things get very bloody, very fast. “They Will Kill You” is stylish, taking cues from Quentin Tarantino, even if it never matches the iconic director’s sharp writing and memorable characters.

#3146. Claude can collaborate in your team meetings soon – like an intern

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude is responding 'Yes' to that calendar invite - with some limitations. Plus: Anthropic launches two more new features that are available now.

Anthropic often refers to its Claude agent as your coworker. Soon, the company said, it will be able to join your meetings like one, and start working on the tasks you and your team are discussing live.

Also: I locked down my OpenClaw agent with Claude Code – then dared it to escape

“Claude Meetings will let you add Claude to a call to take notes and update the documents your team is working on during the conversation,” Anthropic said. The feature, which will be available for Team and Enterprise plans, theoretically goes beyond something like Gemini’s Google Meet transcription and note-taking, which identifies action items but doesn’t proactively contribute to them.

In material shared with ZDNET prior to the launch, the company said Claude “won’t join a call with outside guests unless an admin allows it, and it leaves if one joins anyway.” The company also said Claude Meetings will be on by default for Team plans, but Enterprise admins will be able to choose who gets it. The feature won’t work for organizations with “zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).”

The company did not clarify when Meetings would roll out, but announced several other updates for companies that are available now.

To further keep as much of your work ecosystem within the Claude universe, Anthropic released a new Whiteboards feature in beta.

Also: Claude’s Record-a-Skill cut my research to minutes

“Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time,” Anthropic said. Claude will group crowdsourced notes into themes and action items. Maybe double-check the results of that spew before locking anything in.

After brain-dumping like you might on a physical whiteboard, Anthropic said, Claude can turn that output into a deck or document, or export it to other tools for next steps.

A new Sheets feature is exactly as it sounds: Claude can now create shareable spreadsheets from a prompt and edit inside cells with trackable changes. But it’s not fully replacing the old guard of spreadsheets just yet.

“When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel,” Anthropic said. “You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet.”

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free, local AI stack

Claude Dashboards, which only launched in beta last month, is now called Data. The tool can query company data from large external services such as Amazon Redshift and ClickHouse and comes with tracked changes and faster loading thanks to caching. According to Anthropic, it’s intended to let companies standardize metrics to avoid having conflicting data, surface data stories, and create a live source of truth everyone can access.

“With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access,” the company said.

Anthropic said that for Team plans, all three features are on by default. For Enterprise plans, only Claude Data will be on by default starting Nov. 19. Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, though you can adjust those settings in Artifacts.

Anthropic has maintained a lead over OpenAI by focusing on enterprise clients first, while OpenAI has prioritized several consumer products. Releases like this are unsurprising, as they serve Anthropic’s primary base. Both Anthropic and OpenAI are increasingly branching into workplace and productivity software for large-scale companies. That said, Anthropic’s recent release of a personal finance tool rivals OpenAI’s existing equivalent geared toward consumers.

Also: Claude’s new Personal Finance tool aims to help analyze your spending

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

In September, at its Dev Day, OpenAI released ChatGPT Space, which houses document and slide creation tools reminiscent of Google Workspace. Before that, Anthropic had similarly consolidated its document and slide creation features into a single hub.

If there’s a slight differentiator here versus Google Workspace, it’s interface seamlessness. Anthropic has designed Claude itself as the starting point for a range of workplace deliverables, rather than maintaining distinct applications that can quickly feel siloed.

#3145. Mercedes’ New Point-to-Point Driver Assist Helped Me Overcome My Fear of Driving

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

New hands-free highway and driving-assistance features are coming to select US models next year. I got an early look at the tech to see if it could make me feel more comfortable behind the wheel.

“This can go one of two ways,” I think as I slide behind the wheel. “Either this makes city driving a lot less intimidating, or I regret ever giving it a try.”

As someone who rarely drives – and doesn’t even own a car – in San Francisco, I was eager to see whether Mercedes-Benz’s new point-to-point driving assistance system could ease my anxiety as I navigated the city’s notoriously challenging streets. How would it handle the many four-way stops, steep inclines, pedestrians, cyclists and double-parked robotaxis?

After an hour of weaving through these complex environments, I walked away feeling more at ease than when I started. That’s largely because I barely had to lift a finger – or a foot.

I got an early opportunity to try Mercedes-Benz’s new point-to-point driver assistance system, MB.Drive Assist Pro, which will roll out to select California customers in December before expanding to the rest of the US next year. The Level 2 system handles functions like steering, braking and acceleration, but the driver has to be attentive and ready to take over at any moment. However, I hardly ever needed to.

As I made my way through San Francisco’s Financial District, Marina and North Beach in a Mercedes-Benz GLC 400, I repeatedly had to resist the urge to tap the brakes, press the accelerator or grab the steering wheel out of instinct. But within minutes, my apprehension had given way to awe at just how much the system could handle and how little I needed to do. With MB.Drive Assist Pro engaged, I watched as the vehicle obeyed traffic signals, yielded the right of way and even maneuvered around stalled robotaxis. Occasionally, I had to briefly place my hands on the wheel so it would know I was paying attention, but I didn’t find it bothersome at all.

There were moments when I had to take control. At one intersection, a pedestrian was preparing to cross, but the system persisted in making a right turn. (The death glare I got was a sign I needed to take over and tap the brakes.) Further down the road, I grabbed the wheel to steer around a parked truck unloading cargo. Other times, my patience was tested as the car came to a complete stop at every stop sign (rolling stops are my forte, sorry not sorry). To its credit, though, the vehicle subtly asserted itself at four-way stops by inching forward as we waited for our turn.

Unlike Level 4 robotaxi services like Waymo and Zoox, Level 2 systems like MB.Drive Assist Pro aren’t fully autonomous, but can take some of the stress out of everyday driving, particularly in dense urban environments.

Tesla’s so-called Full Self-Driving (Supervised) offers similar capabilities, navigating city streets, maneuvering around obstacles, making turns, changing lanes and responding to traffic signals, while still requiring driver supervision. Other systems like GM’s Super Cruise, Ford BlueCruise and BMW Highway Assistant offer hands-free driving on compatible roads, but are primarily designed for use on highways rather than complex city streets.

A feature like MB.Drive Assist Pro could not only bring increasingly advanced driver assistance technology to more car owners but also lay the groundwork for a future in which autonomous driving becomes more common in personally owned vehicles.

“We’ve clearly shown that the autonomous driving sector is an area that we will continue to develop and [be] involved in, and being one of the first companies to offer a system like you guys experienced today shows that we’re committed to be in that space and continue to grow,” Jason Hoff, CEO of Mercedes-Benz North America, said during a reporter roundtable following the demos.

MB.Drive Assist Pro uses 27 sensing components, including 10 cameras, five radar sensors and 12 ultrasonic sensors scattered throughout the vehicle. This hardware is currently available on certain 2027 Mercedes vehicles, including CLA Electric, GLE, GLS and S-Class cars. Starting with 2028 models, the company says more of its US passenger vehicles will be equipped to support the new feature.

Nvidia’s Alpamayo Stack powers the vehicle’s autonomous driving capabilities, using AI to interpret complex road scenarios and reason through driving decisions. It works alongside Nvidia’s Halos safety tech, including Halos OS, which provides safety guardrails to help ensure the vehicle follows the rules of the road, like stopping at a red light or waiting for an intersection to clear before crossing.

With Level 2 driving, there’s a mental hurdle that drivers like me will need to overcome and a certain degree of control we’ll have to relinquish to let the system do its thing. For instance, I sometimes found myself getting nervous as the car confidently moved into the oncoming lane to pass a stalled vehicle, even with approaching traffic. I was assured by the Mercedes team that the system can determine whether there’s enough room to safely squeeze through and otherwise wouldn’t attempt the move. Still, it’s not something I’d personally feel comfortable doing if I were in full control.

Some of this simply comes down to a learning curve. Over the hour I spent behind the wheel, I found myself feeling less anxious and more trusting of the system. I’d imagine that confidence would only grow with repeated use of MB.Drive Assist Pro, so drivers can feel less apprehensive about the car taking the lead, even if some decisions still occasionally give them pause.

MB.Drive Assist Pro will be available nationwide starting next year, with one-month, one-year and three-year subscription options. It’ll come to eligible Mercedes-Benz models including the 2026 CLA electric sedan, 2027 CLA sedan, 2027 GLC electric SUV, 2027 GLE SUV and coupe, 2027 GLS SUV and 2027 S-Class sedan. The system launched in China alongside the new CLA in late 2025. The upcoming rollout will bring it to the US and Germany as well.

Customers can factory-order MB.Drive Assist Pro, or purchase it digitally through the Mercedes-Benz store; it will be delivered as an over-the-air update. Mercedes hasn’t yet shared pricing.

Mercedes is also bringing hands-free highway driving to the US in spring 2027. I had the chance to try out that tech early as well, which proved to be an even bigger test of my trust.

As I drove from Alameda, across the Bay from San Francisco, onto Interstate 880 in a GLS 580, I took a deep breath and prepared to hand over some control to the car. After pressing the Resume button on the steering wheel (or adjusting the cruise control speed), I could activate Hands-Free Highway Assist. The feature comes with a few restrictions: you have to be on a freeway, not in an exit lane and away from construction zones or particularly sharp curves. You also can’t be driving faster than 85 mph.

Hands-Free Highway Assist lets you kick back a bit as the vehicle drives, slowing down and speeding up with traffic. A capability called Proactive Lane Change Assist can automatically switch lanes to overtake a slower vehicle or approach an upcoming exit based on the navigation route.

As with MB.Drive Assist Pro, you have to watch the road and be ready to take over at any time while using Hands-Free Highway Assist. Given the high stakes and high speeds, I wasn’t as hands-off with the highway driving feature as I was in the urban environment. Driving on the highway already feels nerve-wracking to me even when I’m in full control, so I couldn’t quite overcome the mental hurdle of letting go, physically and metaphorically, for more than about a minute at a time. I’d activate the feature, panic, then reactivate it. (Clearly, I’m a huge thrill seeker.)

One key hurdle is that it can be difficult to know when Hands-Free Highway Assist has been activated. An icon appears on the dashboard showing a green steering wheel with gray hands and two As on each side when the feature is available. Those hands will disappear when the feature is active, leaving only the green steering wheel and As. The icon turns red when you need to take over. Still, it was a little tricky to tell when the feature had correctly been enabled and when I hadn’t yet met all the requirements. Again, part of this is the learning curve, but it’s a big lesson to learn at 65 mph.

Still, when I was brave enough to activate the feature, it was impressive to witness the vehicle smoothly weaving across lanes on its own and following the flow of traffic, especially when I had the chance to try it again later in the afternoon on the S 580E. It seems like a handy capability that can make long-haul journeys and daily commutes a little less miserable.

Hands-Free Highway Assist will be available in the US in the spring, and pricing has yet to be determined. An early access program will give select California customers the chance to access the feature next month, alongside MB.Drive Assist Pro. Hands-Free Highway Assist will be on vehicles that support MB.OS (Mercedes’ in-house operating system) as part of the MB.Drive Assist offering, which already includes Steering Assist, Lane Change Assist and Proactive Lane Change Assist. The new feature will arrive via an over-the-air update.

After a day of stepping outside my comfort zone in more ways than one, it was fascinating to get a glimpse of where automotive technology is headed – and how it could make everyday drives, even the more stressful ones, feel a little less daunting. But for now, I hopped into an Uber and returned to my usual routine of avoiding the driver’s seat.

#3144. 5 Things to Do if You're Forced to Retire Sooner Than Expected

It's not an ideal situation, but don't panic.

When you build a retirement plan around ending your career at a certain age, and you're forced to exit the labor force sooner, it can constitute a pretty big blow. But it's not totally uncommon to be forced into an earlier retirement due to a layoff, health challenges, or the need to care for a loved one.

The good news is that being pushed out of the workforce ahead of schedule doesn't have to completely upend your long-term plans. Here's how to pivot and salvage the situation.

If you're forced into early retirement due to a layoff, the first thing to do is review your exit package. You may be entitled to severance pay, plus compensation for accrued vacation and/or sick time.

Take the time to review the details of your severance agreement so you know what to expect. Also keep in mind that your agreement may include certain restrictions, so don't just gloss over the fine print.

Being forced into retirement sooner than planned could mean losing your health insurance. If you're not yet 65, you're typically too young for Medicare, which means you'll need to secure coverage on your own.

Take the time to review your options, which may include COBRA if you can afford the premiums or an Affordable Care Act marketplace plan. If your spouse is still working and has insurance through their job, joining that health plan may be the most affordable bet. While you should make sure to compare your choices thoroughly, don't wait, because going without health insurance is inherently risky.

If you're at least 62 when you're forced to retire, it means you're old enough to start collecting Social Security. Whether you should start benefits is a different question.

You won't get your Social Security benefits in full until age 67 if you were born in 1960 or later. And for each year you delay your claim past that point, until age 70, your benefits get a permanent 8% boost.

Filing for Social Security ahead of schedule could reduce a critical income stream for life, so before you do that, assess your retirement savings. You may be able to comfortably withdraw additional money from your IRA or 401(k) for a period of time so you can hold off on taking benefits right away.

Retiring sooner than planned could mean that your savings have to last longer, and that you need to reduce portfolio risk sooner. Take the time to assess your portfolio and make sure you have at least a few years' worth of safe investments, like bonds.

It's also wise to set yourself up with enough cash to cover one to two years of expenses. That way, if you need money when your portfolio is down, you won't have to lock in permanent losses by liquidating assets at a bad time.

If the reason for your forced retirement boils down to being downsized out of a job and you can't find a new one in your field, it doesn't mean your days of working have to end. You may be able to find flexible part-time work that lets you earn some income and stay busy.

Let's say you were earning $8,000 a month at your full-time job. If you're able to find gig work or a part-time role that lets you earn $2,000 a month, you're looking at a $6,000 monthly income shortfall instead of $8,000. Those part-time wages could take some pressure off your savings if you're tapping your IRA or 401(k) sooner than planned.

Just as importantly, having a job to go to could be good for your mental health. Even if you don't necessarily need the money, it could be an option worth pursuing.

Being forced to end your career before you're ready is not an easy situation to cope with. Taking the steps above could help protect your finances as you navigate your new reality.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

More phones are getting Gemini Intelligence, but only Pixel users can access it in a new way.

Gemini Intelligence is spreading beyond the Google Pixel 11 lineup to the Pixel 10, the upcoming Motorola Signature 27, and several of Samsung’s Galaxy foldables and flagship phones.

Though Google often offers its most upgraded features to other Android phone manufacturers, there are some features that are Pixel-exclusive or come to Pixel users first. This time, Gemini Intelligence is coming to Android Auto, but only for eligible Pixel users.

Also: I’m an Android Auto ride or die – but Apple CarPlay beats it on these 3 features

Google’s blog post states that Pixel users with Gemini Intelligence can expect it to gather information from their apps and surface it to their car’s infotainment screen. Google’s example is that if a friend texts you asking where you’re meeting for Pilates, Gemini Intelligence can find the correct confirmation email and offer to send it with one tap.

To access Gemini Intelligence in Android Auto, the Gemini app and subsequent setup are required; it’s available in select countries to users aged 18 and older, and feature availability will vary.

With more context about your messages, emails, and calendar events, a more capable assistant can complete cross-app tasks while driving, such as “remind me to buy mom a birthday card before her birthday” or “which route to my dentist appointment will be the fastest?” I often use Siri AI in CarPlay for tasks like these, and Gemini operates the same way. However, these tasks require user input first; what makes an AI assistant in in-car software great is when it suggests tasks before you ask for them.

Siri suggests to me when I should leave my house for an upcoming event in my calendar, such as a dinner reservation, flight, or doctor’s appointment, based on traffic conditions. It looks like Gemini Intelligence in Android Auto will offer the same assistance. I’ve reached out to Google to confirm, and will update this article if I get a response.

Also: 4 wireless Android Auto adapters we recommend (and they’re cheap)

I find Siri’s upgraded capabilities most useful when I have a busy day and heavy Atlanta traffic is thrown in the mix. Sometimes people need information about where to meet up, but I don’t remember the exact name of the location or which street it’s on. It’s difficult to search through my old messages or emails while staying alert to crazed drivers on the interstate, so a smarter AI assistant comes in handy.

Though Gemini Intelligence in Android Auto is reserved for Pixel users, the upgrade follows a series of improvements Google has rolled out to its in-car software. Non-Pixel Android phones and Android phones without Gemini Intelligence can use Personal Intelligence, which connects Gemini across your Google Maps, Photos, or Gmail data.

Personal Intelligence users can ask Gemini to navigate to a restaurant with a specific cuisine or vibe, or search their photos to find a car wash they photographed last week. Gemini Intelligence is more proactive and expansive, drawing on more sensitive data from your phone, such as messages, while Personal Intelligence relies solely on data from your Google services.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Oura's acquisition of Counsel Health could signal a new dawn for digital care.

Oura has entered into an agreement to acquire AI primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million. The acquisition of Counsel Health, which was already a partner in the Oura app, will give users access to Counsel’s in-house physicians and 24/7 medical AI.

The Oura Ring has evolved from its beginnings as a sleep tracker to what its CEO, Tom Hale, calls “a doctor in your pocket.” The company has its sights set on making the device a continuous medical companion, and Counsel’s acquisition is one way it’s furthering that mission.

Oura employs its 24/7 health monitoring to recognize potential deviations from a user’s biometric baseline, and the partnership will build on those capabilities by adding more clinical guidance through Counsel Health.

The partnership will also connect members with Counsel Health’s medical AI and in-house physicians to address timely health problems, support, or “prescriptions for episodic health conditions,” the press release said. The acquisition offers specialty and chronic care for chronic conditions, like reproductive, aging, and cardiometabolic-related conditions.

“Oura tells members what’s happening in their bodies, and Counsel helps them act on it. This combination expands our addressable market and deepens the value we deliver to every member,” David Shuman, executive chairman of Oura, said in a press release.

This is the third acquisition Oura has made this year, following its acquisition of Galen AI, a conversational and personal health platform that connects smart ring data to medical records, and Doublepoint AI, an AI‑driven, biometric and gesture recognition company that could add voice or gesture controls to Oura’s next smart ring.

Also: Before you buy a smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

The Counsel Health deal is expected to close by the end of the year. It’s unknown whether access to Counsel Health physicians or the 24/7 medical AI will be included in an Oura app subscription.

Tech companies have a growing appetite for health tech startups. Last year, Samsung announced a similar acquisition of Xealth, a care platform that connects more than 500 hospitals with 70 digital health centers. The acquisition, according to Samsung VP of digital health Praveen Raja, furthers Samsung’s mission to connect the healthcare landscape, from symptom detection to care provider connection.

One of the Oura Ring’s superpowers is its ability to detect developing illnesses or deviations from my biometric baseline (a spiked resting heart rate, a higher body temperature) before I feel those symptoms. I’ve written about how my Oura Ring detected an illness earlier this year, one day before I began to feel sick.

Also: I should’ve listened to my Oura Ring when it warned me about my health

When Oura has flagged these concerns to me, I take them seriously, even as my care provider — to whom I show this data — may shrug them off. The Counsel Health acquisition enables medical AI and in-house physicians to contextualize your biometrics when you are sick or managing a chronic condition.

Will this acquisition help ease the demand for urgent care clinics? As a regular visitor to and hater of my Brooklyn CityMD, I hope so. It is notoriously difficult to get a same-day, in-person appointment with a primary care provider in New York because of high demand and a stretched-thin healthcare system, which often leaves urgent care as the only in-person option for patients.

The press release says that users could ask physicians for prescriptions. I’m thinking that if I get another bad cold this winter, I could go to my Oura app for help and symptom management instead of CityMD. Making a physician readily available to Oura users could, in theory, reduce dependence on primary or urgent care providers.

Robert Pattinson is staying booked and busy.

It’s safe to say Robert Pattinson is on a generational run, starring in The Odyssey, The Drama, Die My Love and Primetime just this year alone. Having previously played Edward Cullen in The Twilight Saga and Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves’ The Batman (and gearing up for a role in Dune: Part Three this December), he’s no stranger to major film franchises.

Now he’s adding one more major role to his portfolio: James Bond.

Amazon MGM Studios named the English actor the new 007 on Monday, ending the hunt to replace Daniel Craig, who played Bond from 2006 to 2021 in five films: Casino Royale, Quantum of Solace, Skyfall, Spectre and No Time to Die.

Several other British A-list actors were speculated to be in the running for the role, including Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor, but it seems Amazon MGM Studios is banking on a big-name actor with a proven record of box-office success for its lead. Pattinson’s connection to director Denis Villeneuve, who was also director of the Dune trilogy, likely played a role in the decision, too.

“To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement,” Pattinson said in a statement. “I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Read more: Ready to Watch a James Bond Movie? These Are My Top Recommendations for You

Pattinson is the eighth actor to play James Bond on screen. The full list of actors who have portrayed 007 includes Sean Connery (1962-1983), David Niven for one (unofficial) film in 1967, George Lazenby for one film in 1969, Roger Moore (1973-1985), Timothy Dalton (1987-1989), Pierce Brosnan (1995-2002) and Craig (2006-2021).

The next Bond film has not yet been titled and is not expected to begin filming until 2027, with a 2028 release date. Steven Knight (Peaky Blinders) has been brought on as the screenwriter, with Amy Pascal (Project Hail Mary) and David Heyman (Harry Potter series) producing and Tanya Lapointe (Dune trilogy) executive producing.

Amazon formally closed its acquisition of MGM Studios in 2022 for $8.45 billion, giving it the rights to distribute all James Bond films. In 2025, Amazon MGM Studios announced a joint venture with longtime franchise producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli to remain co-owners of the franchise, while ultimately giving Amazon MGM Studios creative control.

“Few films carry the kind of anticipation that comes with James Bond, and we have strived to honor the passionate fans, the legacy and the future of this iconic character,” said Courtenay Valenti, head of film at Amazon MGM Studios. “We are thrilled to officially welcome Robert Pattinson as our 007 and are confident he will bring something truly special to this role. Robert, Denis, Amy, David and Tanya are embarking on an amazing adventure together.”

#3137. Where Will AMD Stock Be in 5 Years?

AMD can become a multibagger over the next five years.

Shares of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -0.66%) have soared impressively over the past five years, rising by an incredible 244% during this period. However, it is worth noting that the majority of the stock's gains have arrived over the past 18 months.

The stock has simply taken off since May 2025, jumping by 421% and crushing the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite index's 38% gains over the same period. The good news for investors is that AMD stock can deliver substantial gains over the next five years, even after its red-hot rally.

Let's check out AMD's prospects and see where the stock could be after five years.

AMD is gradually becoming a key player in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market, as evident from the company's third-quarter results. Its data center revenue increased by 97% from the year-ago period to a record $8.5 billion. The company is benefiting from the phenomenal demand for its Instinct data center graphics cards and Epyc server processors.

Additionally, AMD has started shipping its Helios rack-scale server solutions to customers. It expects Helios shipments to increase substantially going forward, driven by increased production by AMD's partners. Not surprisingly, AMD expects stronger data center revenue growth in 2027. The company previously expected data center revenue to more than double next year but now expects "data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected 90 days ago."

AMD can sustain healthy data center revenue growth over the next five years considering that capital spending on AI infrastructure could increase from $765 billion in 2026 to $1.64 trillion in 2031. AI chips alone could generate over $1.1 trillion in revenue in 2031, up from $494 billion this year. As AMD gains a larger share of the AI chip market, it will be able to capture a larger share of this lucrative addressable opportunity

Meanwhile, Microsoft and Sony could launch their next-generation gaming consoles in late 2028. AMD is designing the semi-custom processors that power these consoles, which means its gaming segment is likely to step on the gas once again. AMD reported a 40% year-over-year decline in gaming revenue in Q3 to $773 million, citing lower sales of semi-custom processors due to the age of the current console cycle.

However, the ramp-up of a new console cycle has historically been a tailwind for AMD, and the trend could continue as consumers upgrade to new consoles in the next five years.

AMD's earnings per share (EPS) are anticipated to increase by 94% in 2026 to $8.08. The next couple of years point to a significant increase in the company's EPS, according to consensus estimates.

AMD EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

What's more, AMD's long-term EPS growth estimates have moved up impressively this year.

AMD EPS LT Growth Estimates data by YCharts

Assuming the company clocks even 30% EPS growth in the three years after 2028, its EPS could reach $56.24 after five years.

The Nasdaq Composite index has an average price-to-earnings ratio of 39. Assuming AMD trades at 30 times earnings after five years, in line with its five-year average earnings multiple, its stock price could reach $1,687. That's just over 3.3x AMD's current stock price, suggesting that it has the potential to make investors significantly richer over the next five years.

#3136. Google Fi now switches between the best mobile networks automatically – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Networking > Mobile Carriers

Pixel users also get a bonus Wi-Fi upgrade. Here's what to know.

From left to right: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8, Google Pixel 11, Google Pixel 11 Pro XL.

Google Fi wireless customers with Pixel phones just got a serious upgrade to their mobile and Wi-Fi connections for free.

Google has announced two new “super network” connection features for Fi Wireless: one that automatically switches between two of the largest 5G cellular networks, and another that automatically connects to premium Wi-Fi in millions of locations without you needing to log in.

The features are rolling out today for Pixel 9 phones and newer models on every Google Fi plan. If you’re not a current Fi customer, you can sign up for a free seven-day trial to test it alongside your current carrier.

Here’s how the new mobile connection feature works: if your main connection slows or becomes unstable, Fi will automatically move to a secondary connection. This not only means you’ll have the fastest option when your connection is good, but you’ll have fewer dead zones when service is limited.

Also: I compared Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T 5G coverage on a road trip – and the winner surprised me

The feature will run on MEP (Multiple Enabled Profiles) technology, which allows a single eSIM chip to host and run multiple SIM profiles simultaneously. Footnotes in Google’s release note that you’ll need to have “any non-Fi SIMs disabled.”

Google Fi originally offered automatic switching between two networks when the service debuted a decade ago, but it was between Sprint and T-Mobile, which merged in 2020. Google didn’t reveal what the “two of America’s best 5G cellular networks” were, but ZDNET has reached out to ask. The service usually runs on T-Mobile. Along with T-Mobile, the three biggest carriers are AT&T and Verizon, so it’s likely the second carrier is one of those.

In addition to a mobile connection upgrade, users are getting better Wi-Fi, too. Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ will automatically connect you to faster Wi-Fi in millions of locations like airports and malls (Google defines “faster” as two times better reliability and 30% improved latency compared to normal Google Fi cellular networks) without you having to log in or head to your settings. These connections will be automatically encrypted, Google said, keeping your online activity safe.

Also: 6 default Pixel 11 settings I changed that made a big difference – and why

This feature is also coming to Samsung phones running One UI 9 or higher and select modern Motorola phones.

Both of these features, Google explained, are available internationally and are included on Unlimited Premium and Flexible plans at no extra cost.

#3133. A Familiar Setup for Crypto? November 2026 Is Starting to Look a Lot Like November 2022.

The market's late-summer rally off the lows is now looking more like a mirage than something solid to build on.

Sorry to say it, cryptocurrency investors, but crypto's slump into November 2026 looks an awful lot like the crypto winter of November 2022, even though the market got a reprieve in the late summer and early fall. In that last crypto winter in 2022, Bitcoin (BTC +0.90%) fell 77% from its peak, which came right after the FTX crypto exchange collapsed.

So did the crypto bear market really end this summer, or was the excitement just a particularly vigorous bear-market rally that ended up spawning a lot of new, worthless projects? Let's dig into the historical data a bit more and make a determination.

The summer rally looked so convincing at the time that it seemed to portend an exciting new crypto bull market.

Bitcoin gained about 44% in the third quarter and hit $87,395 in the week ended Sept. 27. As of Nov. 16, it has fallen 23% without pausing much along the way, pushing it past the 20% decline that constitutes a bear market. Other leading cryptoassets, like Ethereum (ETH -0.26%), Solana (SOL +5.23%), and Zcash (ZEC +10.64%), have also performed quite badly since then:

The sharp decline of Zcash is particularly troublesome, as it was one of the very few coins that managed to rally during the past 12 months as everything else was falling. It's also one of the assets that many investors, including yours truly, had considered a prime candidate to lead a new bull market, similar to Solana's role in the early phases of the 2023 bull market.

Here, two other echoes of 2022 are so loud that they're hard to ignore.

On Oct. 29, hackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest crypto exchange. In 2022, FTX's collapse delivered the final leg down, pushing Bitcoin to $15,480 by Nov. 22.

Then, on Nov. 10 of this year, October's Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by 0.4% versus the 0.3% expected, and now the market is largely anticipating a Federal Reserve interest rate hike at its next meeting. In November 2022, the Fed raised its benchmark rate range to 3.75%-4%, marking its sixth increase that year. This year, it raised rates to that same range on Sept. 16, then held there on Oct. 28, with two Fed officials dissenting in favor of another increase. Such hiking cycles tend to be toxic for riskier assets like crypto.

This time around, a few of the other details are slightly different.

Binance says it will be able to cover its users' losses from the hack, whereas FTX went bankrupt, and its customers waited more than two years for repayments that began in February 2025. In 2022, the degree of connection between the traditional financial sector and the crypto sector was much weaker.

Today, spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) exist, and they let capital flow from one sector to the other much more freely than before, which could attenuate the intensity of a drawdown -- or perhaps make it worse.

Measured from its September high, Bitcoin is already back in a bear market, so the real question is whether its July 1 low of $57,749 will hold. It's still above that level as of Nov. 16, and I doubt it will break below that, but it's possible.

The more important point here is that if you're an investor with a long-term outlook, as you probably should be, a continuation of the bear market would be an opportunity to look for bargains rather than a cause for despair.

The next recovery could also have a bigger tailwind than before. In June 2026, Citigroup projected that the base of tokenized assets (stocks, bonds, and funds recorded as blockchain tokens) would grow from about $17 billion to reach a value in the ballpark of $5.5 trillion by 2030 in its base case. That money won't lift every coin, though. Bitcoin benefits most directly, as institutions compete for a fixed supply, while Ethereum's and Solana's networks earn fees only when that activity settles on their public chains.

Smaller coins look even riskier than usual given the current backdrop of uncertainty. CoinGecko research in 2025 found that 53.2% of all the cryptocurrencies ever listed on its tracker had failed. Yes, Solana was a small, relatively unknown coin at the start of 2023. But for each Solana, many thousands of tokens went to zero.

Regardless of what happens next with the price of these coins, it's worth accumulating Bitcoin gradually, and if you're a bit more risk-tolerant than the average crypto investor, consider also accumulating Ethereum, Solana, and Zcash as much smaller slices of a diversified portfolio. I suggest avoiding anything outside the top 15 by market value until market conditions improve.

#3132. This tiny box gives your older tech smart home superpowers – and it’s only $69

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home Assistant gets new equipment to battle planned obsolescence and abandoned cloud services.

Home Assistant is perhaps the most versatile smart home automation system of them all, thanks to the extreme customization power it offers. Today, a tiny, new box-shaped device is giving Home Assistant users a way to make their existing electronics smarter, rather than replacing them to keep up with the times.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things

The Home Assistant Connect AUX-2 is a multi-purpose piece of hardware made by Nabu Casa, the company behind official Home Assistant hardware. The device brings together several connectivity options, including RS-232 serial for older TVs and other equipment, and the ability to connect older stereo systems and amplifiers to modern multi-room audio setups.

“The most sustainable device is the one you already own,” said Paulus Schoutsen, founder of Home Assistant and Nabu Casa. “No device should be left behind because it doesn’t have smart capabilities, or worst of all, its cloud services get turned off.

With the AUX-2, Home Assistant is joining the fight against planned obsolescence and abandoned cloud services.

Modern smart home systems have a major drawback: they exclude working electronics simply because they weren’t designed to integrate with today’s smart home platforms. This is the problem that the AUX-2 addresses.

Instead of buying a new stereo system with smart features, consumers can use the $69 AUX-2 to make the devices they already own smarter, more connected, and easier to control.

A single AUX-2 can control multiple devices, depending on how they’re connected and the interfaces they use. The device’s limit has more to do with the number of physical connections required.

Also: How I open-sourced my smart home – and ditched Google for Siri

The AUX-2 lets you connect two serial-controlled devices directly through the RS-232 ports. The USB port can act as an expansion for compatible adapters. You can place one AUX-2 on an entertainment center and connect an older stereo and TV, then use another AUX-2 elsewhere in your house for additional equipment with physical serial connections.

According to Home Assistant, with an AUX-2, you can control an old AV receiver without the original app, have an older TV respond to commands without relying on its manufacturer’s cloud servers, or integrate existing audio equipment into modern multiroom sound systems.

This way, consumers won’t need to trash a functional piece of equipment simply because the manufacturer stops supporting it.

Aside from RS-232 serial, the AUX-2 also supports Bluetooth, Z-Wave, USB, PoE, and Wi-Fi for connectivity.

Xiaomi's bonkers dual-screen phone is here and I've been testing its camera.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Xiaomi is taking the wraps off its phone in Paris tomorrow, but I’ve had the phone for the past few weeks and have been putting the camera to the test in my beautiful home of Edinburgh, Scotland, and in Paris, France. While it’s too early for me to share my full thoughts on the phone and its cameras (keep your eyes peeled tomorrow for that), I did want to share some of my favorite photos I’ve taken with the phone so far.

The images seen here are taken with the phone’s various built-in camera modes, largely the black and white mode, as I love the dramatic, filmic look it produces. They’re presented either as-shot or with minimal exposure adjustments using the phone’s built-in editing tools. Stay tuned for much more information on this phone and its wild second display on the back.

Taken using one of the phone’s built-in color styles, I love the vibrancy in this shot. The reds really pop, while the wider angle of the main camera emphasizes the tunnel effect of the alleyway, drawing the eye to the person and their dog.

I may be spoiling the rest of the images here by saying that this is my absolute favorite shot I’ve taken, but there we go. I took this using one of the dedicated black-and-white modes, and I think the tones here are perfect. Excellent dynamic range and contrast, and just the right amount of film grain. I positioned the figure between the buildings and had the phone almost on the floor to turn the rain-soaked tiles into a reflective surface to add some drama to this scene. I then applied a wide cinematic crop in post to give it that extra edge. Lovely stuff.

Most of my favorite photos with the phone were taken using the black-and-white mode. It’s no surprise; I shoot in black and white very often on my Leica Q3 43, and I used the monochrome mode for my favorite shots with Xiaomi’s Leitzphone earlier in the year.

The phone captures excellent black-and-white photos at night, too.

And by exposing for the bright highlights in this scene, I was able to create this stark, moody image of my handsome orange cat, Toulouse. Is he the best cat you’ve ever seen? Of course he is.

Back in color, this UFO that had presumably crash-landed in this Parisian market looks great in this filmic color mode. The oranges and reds pop against the other tones in this scene.

While this quick street portrait is similarly punchy.

I used manual mode here, taking full control over the white balance and exposure settings to achieve the tones I wanted. It’s a great-looking shot with excellent dynamic range. Xiaomi’s phone doesn’t appear to go too hard with its software processing either, meaning that even fine details look quite natural. Other Android phone-makers could take note.

As with the photo of Toulouse the cat, I exposed for the highlights here, forcing the rest of the scene under this bridge into shadow. As a result, it looks moody and dramatic but crucially it also looks exactly as I hoped it would. Many phones would try to artificially lift the shadows here, which would ruin the vibe I was going for.

I took this with the phone’s telephoto zoom lens, aiming to focus more on the digger as the subject and use the water for reflection. I love how this shot looks, especially in black and white, as the cloud detail behind it is especially noticeable.

While here I used the full wide angle of the main camera in order to create a lot of negative space around the figures, emphasizing the size of the building around them.

That building was Le Grande Arche in Paris and despite it being a miserably cold, wet and cloudy day I think the phone has captured a satisfyingly stark scene here.

I don’t like flying, so I distracted myself on the flight out to Paris by taking photos of things with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, including this man having a look out of the window.

And this shot of my plane’s wing somewhere above the UK. Again, in black and white. When it looks this good, why would I choose anything else?

And while we’re still in black and white, a particularly friendly pigeon. Hi, friend!

And to round us off, this dude in shades looking at a menu.

I’m genuinely really thrilled with so many of the shots I’ve taken with this phone. The black-and-white mode in particular is spectacular, and I’m looking forward to taking more shots with it. Stick around for more details on the phone — including the full review — coming soon.

The Spatial Sleep Headband uses audio resonance therapy to improve your sleep but it's an uphill climb to get there. Vibrating your skull while filling your brain with unusual noises, the first few nights are rough going, but it does eventually pay off... slightly. The soothing noises became a pleasant bedtime addition but any sleep changes were minimal. At $319, it's a heavy investment in tech that takes a while to show results.

Clinical research suggests it can help insomnia

First few weeks are disruptive to your sleep

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When you can't sleep, you'll try anything to drift off. But I can almost guarantee you've never tried something like the Spatial Sleep Headband. This peculiar wearable uses acoustic resonance to send you snoozing. I put it to the test and yes, it's as weird as it sounds.

Type: Sleep headbandBest for: Insomnia, trouble falling asleepDimensions: 4" x 7.8" x 3.7"Weight: 2.5 ozWarranty: 90 days limitedPrice: $319 at SoundHealth

The Spatial Sleep Band sits on your forehead where it vibrates and plays sound. With regular use this combo should train your brain's neural response to build better sleep, no hard work required. Although I'll be honest, the Spatial Sleep Band isn't what I'd describe as easy.

I used the Spatial Sleep headband nightly for four weeks and I'll dive into my full experience below. In brief, it's an odd sensation and one that comes with a steep learning curve. And while eventually the Spatial Sleep Band does become a soothing addition to your bedtime routine, it's a struggle to get to that point.

As someone with only mild sleep issues, I've yet to see any real benefit from the Spatial Sleep Band. And the adjustment period was frustrating enough that I'd have given up if it wasn't my job to keep going. For those with more severe sleep problems, the annoyance of the Spatial Sleep Headband will likely feel like less of an intrusion, and the benefits more noticeable.

But it's an expensive gamble, with a Spatial Sleep Headband costing $319 (although that's slightly more affordable than similar sleep headbands like the Muse S Athena and the Elemind). You do get a 45-day return period as well, and by that point you should have a good idea if this product is for you. And it's subscription-free — that's rare for this kind of sleep tech.

The Spatial Sleep Headband costs $319 — an investment, for sure, but this is a fairly standard price tag for a high-tech sleep aid. There's no subscription required and a 45-day returns policy is included.

The overall design of the Spatial Sleep Headband is relatively simple. The slim band is made from a soft material and the Velcro strap is easy to adjust.

Its secret lies on the inside, where you'll find two purple nodules. These press against the forehead and deliver the acoustic vibration that makes the Spatial Headband work.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There's one more important part to the Spatial and that's the three lines on the front of the design. These are used to align the band with the center of your face, to ensure the sound is delivered to the right part of the forehead.

I used the Spatial Sleep Headband for four weeks as part of my usual routine, wearing it to bed (with an eye mask). Here's how I rate the performance...

Setting up the Spatial Sleep Headband is simple, for a piece of complex tech. First you have to charge it, then turn the headband on (there's a button on the front) and connect it to the app.

You'll be asked to scan your face — this helps Spatial create a sound just right for you. When you're ready to sleep, get the band in position and press start on the app.

The sound automatically plays for 45 minutes, at which point you should be asleep (fingers crossed). You can pause and restart the sound from the app, in case of late night wake ups.

The battery lasts for roughly 90 minutes, or two sessions, and I have used mine through two nights without charging. However, I recommend charging after every session, to avoid the sound cutting out. A USB-C cable is provided and charging takes roughly 30 minutes.

The app is mostly used to kick off the audio at night, but there's a fun memory game you can play as well.

I'm normally game for testing any kind of weird sleep tech but when I first strapped the Spatial Band to my head, I felt like I'd made a terrible mistake. Nodules pressed into my forehead and my bones rattled to a dissonant hum that sounded like pans clattering to the ground in the distance. I clenched my jaw and waited for it to end.

There was an important lesson here, echoed in the bright red dents on my forehead: do not over-tighten the band.

With a slightly looser band, night two went better. But the first week was rough. The sound and sensations of the Spatial Headband are far removed from my usual sleep comforts. I was hoping using it would help me drift off quickly but instead I lay awake, questioning the life choices that had led me to this moment.

Spatial does warn that it takes persistence before you see results and week two went better. The sound and I had gotten used to each other, meaning it no longer sat at the forefront of my mind. Now I enjoyed a pleasant background hum and only occasionally worried about my vibrating skull.

By week three I could see a glimmer of progress. The distant drone of the sleep headband had grown relaxing. One night, on the brink of sleep, I even found myself wondering what the pleasant noise was.

These benefits have yet to be reflected in my sleep score, however. On some nights it still takes me up upwards of 30 minutes to drift off fully. And I'm still experiencing brief wake ups in the night. (Including waking up to take the headband off — the nodules are uncomfortable when they press against your face.)

Last night, having reached the end of my four weeks testing period, I decided to ditch the headband and go back to my usual sleep patterns. I got an 88 sleep score from my Oura Ring, my highest in 12 nights.

As someone with only minor sleep problems, the Spatial Sleep Headband is a steep learning curve for a small advantage. But I don't want to write it off entirely. There are strong reviews from other users and Spatial has conducted some notable research. Spatial is designed to improve your natural sleep frequency, so for those who have a sleep routine that's completely off-beat, the Spatial sleep might help set the pace you need.

The Spatial Headband uses acoustic vibrations and sleep-friendly frequencies to improve the quality and quantity of your sleep. It requires regular use to see the results and after several weeks the strange hum of the Spatial should be the backdrop to a decent night's rest.

The problem is that those first weeks are challenging, to put it mildly. From the sound to the feel, the Spatial band is simply strange to use. It feels like a disruptive force and you might be tempted to give up before you feel the benefits. Or rather, if you feel the benefits — I stuck with mine and noticed only minor differences.

✅ You're experiencing long-term sleep deprivation: The Spatial Sleep Headband didn't work for me but it is backed by some serious research. Its impact might be more noticeable when overcoming bigger sleep problems.

✅ You've tried all kinds of sleep tech and nothing works: Acoustic resonance is unusual and not the kind of sleep enhancer you pick up on a whim. If you're struggling to improve your sleep, this might be worth a try.

✅ You're kept awake by disruptive noise: When the Spatial band is on, it drowns out most other sounds. That's good news if traffic or rowdy neighbors are contributing to your sleep problems.

❌ You want a quick solution: Spatial suggests it takes three to four weeks to feel the benefit of the Sleep Headband, and I found week one to be a steep learning curve. The Muse S Athena sleep headband was much easier to get used to.

❌ You share a bed with a light sleeper: Some sound does leak from the Spatial headband which might disturb co-sleepers.

❌ You want a small sleep boost, rather than a total overhaul: For minor sleep issues the Spatial Sleep Band is a pricey investment that takes time to get used to. Try low-cost options like sleepy tea and guided meditations before diving in with the Spatial.

The Muse S Athena uses your brainwaves to track your sleep and, when it senses you're about to be disturbed, plays a sleep-inducing sound to send you back under. I tested it and found the performance impressive but it is a premium buy, retailing for $479.99 at Muse and Amazon.

The Snoozeband isn't as high-tech as the other options listed here but this comfortable set of sleep headphones can help you drift off in noisy environments. It utilizes thin speakers in a soft headband to deliver sleep sounds without the discomfort of an earbud. From $49.99 at Snoozeband.

#3129. If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

This month’s security update is failing on some systems already running the preview update released in October. But there is a fix afoot.

Ah, Microsoft. Another Windows update, another glitch. This latest one affects some Windows 11 users who attempt to install this week’s November Patch Tuesday update, only for it to fail. But don’t worry, there’s already a fix in play.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up – here’s how

On its support page to the November update designated KB5132061, Microsoft revealed and explained this latest problem.

Windows users who installed the November preview update released on October 28 may run into a glitch when trying to install the actual November update released on November 10. In this case, the installation may fail to complete. Your PC might repeatedly try to install the update or you may simply see an error code such as 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993.

I can confirm the problem. I installed the preview update on one of my Windows 11 virtual machines. Trying to then install the actual November update triggered the installation error.

If you’re in the same boat, what can you do to fix this dilemma? Just be patient.

Also: Windows finally gets a built-in internet speed test tool – how to try it

Microsoft promises that all affected PCs should receive repairs within 24 to 48 hours starting from November 11, 1pm ET. For this, make sure your PC is connected to the internet and is set up to receive updates via Windows Update. Head to Settings and select Windows Update. You may already find the November update known as 2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974) available again. If so, select it to install it, and the process should work now.

I tried this on my virtual machine, and the November update installed without a hitch. But if you still bump into errors, check out Microsoft’s support page on troubleshooting problems updating Windows.

Microsoft typically releases each monthly Windows update in two phases.

First, there’s an optional preview update that kicks off around the end of the previous month. This one is considered a non-security update because it contains only feature changes. In this case, the preview update for November was released on October 28. Labeled KB5127936, this one unveiled the new customizable right-click menu, Cloud rebuild option, and other feature changes.

Also: You can change Windows settings directly from a search now

Second, there’s the actual mandatory Patch Tuesday update that contains both security patches and the non-security changes. Here, the November KB5132061 update was rolled out on November 10.

The preview updates are designed for IT administrators, software testers, and others who want an early look. That means they aren’t always fully baked and may contain a few bugs. But since they pop up in Windows Update, anyone can install them.

The actual Patch Tuesday updates are for all Windows users. In this case, there seemed to be an incompatibility or other conflict between the two updates that Microsoft then had to resolve.

I used to save poached eggs for lazy weekends. This microwave method made them part of my weekday routine.

My weekday breakfasts used to come down to a protein smoothie or scrambled eggs, mostly because both are fast.

Poached eggs, my favorite version, stayed on the weekend list because the stovetop method takes more babysitting than I can manage before work. A microwave was the key to changing all that.

Now, with just a small bowl of cold water and about a minute of cooking, I get a poached egg with a firm white and a soft yolk, ready to slide onto toast or greens. And it’s the best prep method I’ve found thus far.

This method demands just one minute, one bowl and leaves no mess, save for the quick rinse of a wet mug. The results are surprisingly good and the process is impossible to flub. You can easily tinker with timing to get the exact consistency you’re after.

So ditch the frying pan or sluggish pot of boiling water. Here’s how to make perfect poached eggs in under 60 seconds.

Read more: Achieve Your Daily Protein Goals With This Simple Visual Guide

Step 1: Fill a ramekin with a half-cup of salted, room-temperature water. It must be enough to submerge the egg.

You’ll want enough water to submerge the egg but not spill over the top of the ramekin.

Step 2: Crack one egg and carefully drop it into the water, trying not to disturb its structural integrity.

Step 3: Place the ramekin in the microwave and cook on high for about 45 seconds, longer if you prefer a firmer yolk.

Cook the submerged egg for 40 seconds for a runny yolk and closer to a minute for a firm one.

Step 4: Remove the egg gently from the water with a slotted spoon or wire skimmer.

Lift your egg carefully out of the water with a slotted spoon or mesh strainer.

Step 5: Serve over toast or a bed of greens with avocado, hot sauce, chili crisp and other accompaniments.

In one or two tries you’ll be able to fine-tune your poached egg to your perfect doneness and then nail it every time.

Note: The base temperature for any microwave will vary, and thus, cook times may also. Try 40 to 45 seconds for your first effort, then add five-second increments for subsequent tries until you achieve the desired doneness.

I haven’t experienced any egg-related explosions, but a Reddit deep dive into microwave egg poachers unearthed a nugget of advice: Avoid yolk explosions by poking it through with a toothpick.

Stick that fluffy puff of protein on a piece of toast with some spinach, top it all with flaky salt, hot sauce or hollandaise and have a cafe-quality breakfast in less time than it takes to brew coffee. You can also use them to top a salad or serve over rice with pickled vegetables and chili crisp for a light lunch.

Cooking bacon in the oven is the cleanest method and results in even crispier strips, with no greasy stovetop to clean afterward. A fast water boil with these two pantry ingredients lifts stubborn stains from your best cookware without all the manic scrubbing. Here are nine more cooking hacks that save time, energy, and money.

If you don’t want to cook, this is my favorite prepared meal delivery service for 2025.

A small batch of bacon cooked in the air fryer can be another quick protein value add to your breakfast in the morning and it’s a perfect pairing with your microwave-poached egg.

You can prevent your egg yolk from exploding by starting with a small increment of time in the microwave, like 45 seconds. If you need to heat the egg more, you can add increments of five seconds as needed. Poking the egg yolk with a toothpick before putting the egg in the microwave may also help prevent an explosion during or after poaching the egg.

Using your microwave to poach eggs is a quick way to get some protein added to your breakfast or lunch, and it’s a completely safe way to cook the egg as long as you add small increments to the microwave timer.
