#3127. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3124. iPhone Duo Gets a Facial Unlock Feature, but It’s Not Face ID. What to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Unlocking Apple's foldable should get a lot easier, but there are some caveats.

One of the iPhone Duo‘s biggest drawbacks has just been addressed – mostly.

Unlike Apple’s other current iPhones, the iPhone Duo lacks Face ID, meaning you have to rely on the noticeably less speedy Touch ID or enter a passcode to unlock the foldable device. This would be less painful if the Duo didn’t cost $1,999, and if Face ID hadn’t long been a standard feature across the company’s other iPhones, including its most affordable option.

Now, there’s something of a fix. In its latest iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple has added an option to unlock the iPhone Duo using the front camera. This should make accessing the phone’s contents more seamless and intuitive.

Until now, my least favorite aspect of using the iPhone Duo has been the inability to unlock using facial recognition – a limitation that stands in stark contrast to the foldable phone’s premium feel. Scanning a fingerprint with Touch ID not only feels antiquated for such a pricey device, but also rather slow. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, by contrast, has a facial recognition feature, as well as fingerprint unlocking that’s much faster than the Duo’s.

It appears Apple heard our cries and is bringing a workaround to the Duo. This new unlocking capability isn’t quite the same as Face ID, a more secure biometric facial recognition and authentication system. Instead, the iPhone Duo will now let you unlock the phone using the selfie camera under slightly more limited conditions to help ensure security.

Read more: Meet the Custom-Built Machine That Has Folded the iPhone Duo 500,000 Times

To enable the new optional unlock feature, go to your Duo’s Settings and toggle it on under Touch ID & Passcode. Because unlocking with the Duo’s front camera isn’t as secure as using Touch ID or Face ID, you’ll need to use Touch ID or enter a passcode after around 45 minutes of inactivity. Touch ID is also required when using Apple Pay or accessing your passwords.

Unlocking with the front camera is possible because of a new capability in Apple silicon called Secure Exclaves. The iPhone Duo uses this to securely and privately process data of a user’s face and verify the match. That means iOS, apps, users and Apple can’t access the data used to unlock the phone via the front camera.

I admittedly didn’t think this update would arrive on Apple’s first-generation foldable; I assumed we’d just have to cross our fingers and hope for Face ID to land on the next iteration. It’s a relatively small improvement, but one that I think will make the Duo experience a lot more convenient and in line with the phone’s modern design and aesthetics, even if it’s not a full Face ID fix. As much as I thought I could make do with Touch ID, it turned out to be more of a nuisance than I’d anticipated; I’m so used to the speediness of unlocking by simply looking at a phone’s screen and swiping up. So I’m glad there’s a software update to help address that gap on the Duo.

The next iOS 27.3 developer beta also adds the option for the iPhone Duo to automatically lock when someone closes the phone. You can enable this under Settings > Display & Brightness.

Alongside other recent software updates, including the addition of Reachability to make the Duo’s cover screen content easier to access one-handed, and support for Apple Pencil with USB-C, Apple appears poised to continue rolling out features that make the Duo more adaptable.

Several of the tracker’s best features require Bluetooth 6.0-compatible device.

Google’s Pixel Tag, the company’s take on an Android-exclusive Bluetooth tracker, is finally here, following its August announcement during the Google I/O developer conference.

Also: Google’s new Android XR glasses have lower ‘creep factor’ than competitors

Pixel Tag is a complete Bluetooth tracker for Android users that appears less confined to device-specific ecosystems than Samsung’s Smart Tag 3 and Apple’s AirTag.

However, if you look at Google’s footnotes, the Pixel Tag’s functionality is diminished when an older Android phone is involved. Several of the tracker’s best features require a compatible device running Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, according to Google.

Android 9 and newer encompasses a lot of devices, but Bluetooth 6.0 and newer doesn’t. Here’s what to check before you buy.

Smartphones began shipping with Bluetooth 6.0 in 2025, starting with the Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus and Galaxy S26 Ultra. The following phones also have Bluetooth 6.0:

If your Android phone is older than any of the listed above, even by a generation, it likely supports Bluetooth 5.3 or 5.4 — not enough for the Pixel Tag’s best features.

The Pixel Tag’s precision-finding capabilities are powered by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, a key feature introduced in Bluetooth 6.0. Nearly every review I’ve seen of the Pixel Tag, including our own, tests the tracker when paired with a Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 11, or Pixel 11 Pro.

I assume that Android users whose phones run Android 9.0+ but lack Bluetooth 6.0+ can use the Pixel Tag for very basic, general location tracking. These users may see the tracker’s general location, but Google’s device compatibility footnote appears several times throughout its press release.

The following features require Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, according to Google’s release:

So, on older Android devices without Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, the following aren’t supported: locating the exact direction and distance of your tracked devices, pinging a tracker when you don’t see it, or giving your tracked devices a custom name.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Additionally, shorter-distance tracking requires an ultra-wideband chip inside your Android phone. Channel Sounding handles distance and direction at longer ranges, while UWB takes over for shorter ranges. Most premium Android phones with Bluetooth 6.0 also have UWB chips, but several of Google’s base-model phones lack a UWB chip.

Samsung’s base-model, A-series, and Z Flip-series phones also lack UWB, resulting in more phones that can’t access the Pixel Tag’s short-range precision finding capabilities.

With all the specs in mind, the Pixel Tag is the best option for users of recent premium flagship Android phones. Those without the latest Bluetooth connectivity will find that the Pixel Tag works like any other Bluetooth tracker, with basic functionality.

Also: These are the closest things to AirTags for Android users

The good thing is that a single Pixel Tag is $30, so it’s not much more expensive than a Tile Tag, and cheaper than a Chipolo Loop. Still, if your phone doesn’t support Bluetooth 6.0, you might be better off looking for a cheaper option until you’re ready to upgrade.

#3122. Why a Data Center Slowdown Would Reach Utilities and Electrical Suppliers Before Chipmakers

If the data center build-out starts to hit delays and speed bumps, it will affect the various industries involved differently.

Voters across the United States supported restrictions on data center development or rejected proposals favoring new projects in 40 of 41 local ballot contests on Nov. 3, according to Ballotpedia. The results included five full construction bans and three six-month moratoriums, raising the likelihood that some planned data centers will be delayed or canceled.

A slowdown in construction could reduce future infrastructure spending by electric utilities and cut into orders for electrical equipment.

However, chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA -1.39%) could continue selling chips to existing data centers and new projects in other locations. Hence, the earliest signs of a slowdown in the build-out may appear in electricity contracts and equipment orders rather than chip sales.

Data center developers often request electricity capacity from utilities while their projects are still in the planning stages. However, not all of these requests lead to actual construction.

Developers initially requested more than 30,000 megawatts of electricity capacity from American Electric Power's (AEP -0.36%) Ohio subsidiary. After American Electric Power Ohio introduced requirements for paid engineering studies and binding financial commitments, requests totaling 13,023 megawatts proceeded to studies. Developers had signed new contracts for only 5,642 megawatts by February 2026. Another 12,219 megawatts had already been contracted before American Electric Power Ohio's new data center tariff took effect in July 2025.

This does not mean actual electricity demand declined. Instead, many developers that initially requested power capacity did not proceed with binding contracts. A similar reduction in new commitments could signal slower future construction without immediately affecting electricity sales to existing customers.

Growing electricity demand from data centers can create new investment opportunities for utilities. Large projects may require new power plants, substations, and transmission lines, allowing regulated utilities to earn returns on additional infrastructure investments.

This opportunity is reflected in American Electric Power's expansion plans. The company expects 84 gigawatts of incremental contracted load by 2031. To support that growing demand, the company plans to invest about $100 billion from 2027 through 2031, primarily in power generation, transmission, and distribution. These investments are expected to increase its rate base, or the value of regulated assets on which it can earn returns, to $162 billion by 2031.

However, if some of those planned data centers are delayed or canceled, American Electric Power may need to postpone some of its own infrastructure investments. This could slow its earnings growth, although lower capital spending would also reduce its borrowing needs. Hence, a reduction in new data center projects would affect utilities' future growth opportunities before reducing their current electricity sales.

Data center construction also drives demand for transformers, switchgear, and other electrical equipment. If new projects are delayed, suppliers could receive fewer orders while continuing to deliver equipment already booked.

Eaton (ETN +0.10%) manufactures electrical equipment used in data centers and other industries. In the third quarter, it reported that orders from data center customers across its electrical businesses more than doubled over the preceding 12 months.

Eaton ended the third quarter with $26.2 billion in firm orders awaiting delivery. About 72% of these orders are targeted for delivery within the next 12 months. The backlog includes orders from industries other than data centers.

Hence, a slowdown in new orders might not immediately affect Eaton's revenue. However, if orders continue weakening, the company could eventually face slower sales growth and lower factory utilization.

At its Nov. 12 closing price, Eaton traded at about 26 times its expected 2026 adjusted earnings. Slower earnings growth could put pressure on this valuation. However, demand from utilities, industrial customers, and aerospace could help offset weakness in its data center business.

Chipmakers may not face the same immediate impact from delayed data center construction. Their customer will likely continue to buy chips to upgrade existing facilities or install them at other locations with available electricity and cooling capacity.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal third-quarter results on Nov. 17. The company was guiding for total revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, up from $96.2 billion in the second quarter. However, its actual results will provide a more recent indicator of demand for its artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

Microsoft (MSFT -1.28%) has already demonstrated how chip spending could remain strong despite data center construction delays. In its recently reported quarter, Microsoft's capital expenditures totaled $45.2 billion. Approximately three-quarters of this spending was for shorter-lived assets such as CPUs, GPUs, memory, and storage. This spending continued despite delays in third-party data center capacity.

However, prolonged construction delays could eventually affect chip demand, as new servers require sufficient power and cooling capacity. Nvidia had $279 billion in supply and manufacturing capacity commitments at the end of July, although some agreements can be adjusted before becoming firm orders. If customers delay chip purchases due to limited data center capacity, Nvidia could face risks associated with these commitments.

Hence, Nvidia's upcoming results and management's outlook could help investors assess whether data center construction delays are beginning to affect semiconductor demand.

#3121. John Mulaney’s SNL Sister Eldercare Ad Is an Instant, Painful Classic

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

How long did it take you to text it to your sibling group chat?

Did SNL just add another legendary fake commercial to the show’s hall of fame? On Saturday night, host John Mulaney and the cast delivered a winning pretaped parody commercial that hit a nerve in more than a few households.

In the ad, Mulaney and others fret about their aging parents. Nursing homes don’t appeal, yet in-home care would cost too much. Fortunately, Mulaney has heard about Sister, “a live-in, 24/7 eldercare provider that is completely free, and also your sister.”

“I love my mom more than anything,” says another adult son, played by Andrew Dismukes. “That doesn’t mean I want to help her in the bathroom. Sister doesn’t either. But she will, whereas I won’t. That’s the Sister difference!”

Jane Wickline plays a frantic sister who drops everything, quits her job, breaks her lease, and moves halfway across the country to take care of her elderly dad (Tommy Brennan, ironically one of the youngest cast members).

Mulaney says he just had to text his sister, “Dad fell,” and voilà, she instantly appeared.

Mikey Day plays a doctor who, as the author of the astutely named book Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care, explains how it works.

“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow, not yours,” Day says. “Next, your text arrives, instantly activating her. And that’s it! You’re done for life! See you at the funeral!”

Anyone who’s ever had to care for elderly parents can relate to Sister’s duties: Making those torturous, endless calls to doctors, insurance companies and pharmacists, all while screaming, “Speak to human!” at unhelpful phone trees.

Meanwhile, Kenan Thompson rejoices that he’s still in the will despite doing nothing, and Mulaney and Brennan bond over griping about Sister’s diet restrictions. Mulaney urges viewers to sign up now for the free addition of Sister’s Husband, who just doesn’t know why this burden has to fall on his (defensive) wife.

A quickly flashed line at the end of the ad notes, “Offer void if Sister has a good therapist,” who’d presumably tell her to insist her brothers do their share.

It wasn’t just a fictional sketch to some SNL viewers on Reddit.

“This isn’t funny, this is life for a lot of women,” wrote one person.

“I watched this skit earlier today with my husband, and I started crying,” said another. “It’s exactly the situation I’m in while my brother travels the world.”

The point of the ad is that the duties fell on one very human family member. But tech companies are increasingly eyeing that responsibility as an opportunity for AI or robotic help — if that’s something you and your family are willing to try.

One device we’ve seen is a companion robot, ElliQ, that’s meant to live with elderly family members and serve as a digital assistant, social companion and health advocate. (We tried it out with some of our parents and grandparents.) And a 2025 University of Michigan survey found that older adults often find AI smart home devices and voice assistants useful in helping them age in place. CNET also has a roundup of the most reliable smart tech to help people age in place.

No robot or AI can replace the personal touch and self-sacrificial dedication of Sister. I haven’t replayed an SNL parody commercial this many times since the now-classic 2017 ad for Alexa Echo Silver: For the Greatest Generation.

And yes, I texted the Sister ad to my two sisters (but not my brothers).

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Google is moving digital keys out of individual smart lock apps and into the Google Wallet.

Google is adding digital home keys to Google Wallet, letting users tap their phones to unlock compatible smart locks. The home key functionality, which will integrate with Google Home, will roll out this month.

Also: This tiny box gives your older tech smart home superpowers

Apple introduced Home Keys in 2021 with iOS 15, allowing users to store digital keys in the Apple Wallet. This lets you tap your iPhone or Apple Watch on the lock to unlock it. More recently, the addition of Express Mode to Apple Home lets users unlock smart locks without first unlocking their iPhones with Face ID.

Google’s digital keys use tap-to-unlock via NFC on smart locks. Like the Apple Home Key, you don’t need to unlock your phone to use your digital key, though you can change your verification settings as you wish.

Google’s announcement confirms that the company is embracing Aliro and UWB unlocking technologies as well. UWB unlocking for smart locks is supported on Google Pixel 10 Pro and newer models, as well as select UWB-enabled Samsung Galaxy phones. Aliro is a common standard for compatible smart locks and devices.

Before Google’s announcement, compatible smart locks could be controlled on Android through their accompanying app and Google Home. Smart lock companies also offered their own digital access methods, like NFC cards, Bluetooth, and geolocation.

One digital key will be created for each Google Home, so it can unlock all compatible smart locks in that home. You won’t need to search through digital keys in Google Wallet to find the one for your front door, back door, or bedroom door — just tap your phone and Google Home will recognize the lock as one in your smart home ecosystem.

At launch, Google Wallet will support digital keys for the Aqara U400 with UWB and NFC, and NFC on the Schlage Sense Pro and Nuki Keypad 2.

Google Wallet already supports digital car keys for compatible vehicles.

#3116. Voyager 1 Will Be a Full Light-Day From Earth on Wednesday

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

One of NASA’s longest-running missions is about to become the first human-made object a light-day from Earth, nearly 50 years after launch.

NASA’s Voyager 1 left Earth on Sept. 5, 1977, carrying a camera, a set of science instruments and a gold-plated record of sounds and images from home. Forty-nine years later, it’s about to reach a distance no spacecraft has reached before: one light-day, or roughly 16.1 billion miles. At that range, light needs a full 24 hours to make the trip between Earth and the probe. NASA expects Voyager 1 to cross the line on Nov. 18, nearly five decades into a mission originally planned to last about five years.

It’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to walk that distance.

Fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster than that. It currently zips along the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

The milestone comes 14 years after its previous one, when Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the point where the sun’s heliosphere ends, and entered interstellar space. It’s also 28 years after passing Pioneer 10 to become the human-made object that has traveled the farthest into space.

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the life of Voyager 1. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s life-span.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called The Big Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

It was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for any signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

All of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three remaining instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two instruments still in operation.

Making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

When Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, the RTGs now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

The same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

Thanks to the vastness of space, Voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

#3115. ‘We need more reviewers’: Finding Linux bugs is easy now – fixing them is another story

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Some Linux maintainers are quitting under the crushing strain of AI bug reports, while others see signs for hope.

Recently, Microsoft’s FORGE Lab reported that its AI scanning system, MDASH, turned up 59 upstream Linux kernel bug reports, including one flaw at least 21 years old. That’s less impressive than it sounds. For 2026, through Nov. 2, the Linux Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) team reported an average of 27 CVEs a day.

Why so many? Easy: in Linux, any bug can be a security bug. As Linux Torvalds told me in 2024, “Bugs will happen, and anything can be a security bug if somebody is clever enough to just figure out how to abuse it.” Besides, since Linux runs everything from smartphones to refrigerators to supercomputers, what may be a serious bug in one device may not even appear at all on another.

It’s not just Linux, though. In the latest Windows Patch Tuesday security release, Microsoft reported 726 CVEs. The vast majority of these bug reports are coming from AI programmers. Finding bugs on anything is no longer the hard part. But reviewing and fixing them is, and both Microsoft developers and kernel maintainers are struggling to keep up.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

As the FORGE Lab said, “Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance.” Turning its findings into reports took more than four person-months because “human effort [is] the bottleneck.”

That’s hurting the overworked maintainers. On Nov. 10, an ARM engineer and Linux kernel maintainer Lorenzo Stoakes gave up reviewing code. He’d been a reviewer for the memory-management core, misc, reclaim, and Rust-related sections. Stoakes, a kernel contributor since 2014,  wrote, “Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain.”

Stoakes added, “Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse. At first it was once in a while that I’d see slop. Then it was at least once a week. Then every few days. Nowadays it’s pretty much half of what I see, if not more.”

Also: Filing bugs for open-source apps is a huge help for devs – and easier than you think

He’s not alone. As Greg Kroah-Hartman, the Linux kernel stable maintainer, said in a Q&A session at Open Source Summit Europe, “We don’t have enough people to review them, the onslaught of the LLM-generated patches. We need more reviewers. We don’t have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years.”

It’s not all doom and gloom, though. Linux Torvalds, Linux’s creator, said in a recent Linux Kernel Mailing List (LKML) message that much of the new code in the Linux 7.4 rc 2 “was driven by various AI fixes.”

He continued, “that on the bpf [Berkeley Packet Filter]- side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true. I think most other areas haven’t reached that point yet, but it’s at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn. Don’t hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we’ll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.”

We can but hope. In an interview, Kroah-Hartman isn’t so optimistic. “We are getting closer, yes, but not quite there yet.”  He’s not even willing to give a guesstimate of when human-approved AI fixes will catch up with and overcome AI bug reports.

Also: I locked down my OpenClaw agent with Claude Code – then dared it to escape

Daniel Steinberg, the creator of the open-source cURL project, is also cautiously optimistic. Steinberg, who’s been especially critical of AI slop bug reports, told me in an interview that he now believes “we manage the flood pretty well so far, even if it goes a little up and down in periods depending exactly on who sends us a new set of findings this particular week.”

Still, while AI bugs remain a major headache for now, AI bug fixes, along with the work of thousands of maintainers, may finally be starting to stem the AI bug flood. I still foresee long days and nights of work ahead.

I also expect we’ll see more serious security breaches. In November alone, we saw a serious Linux TCP networking security hole revealed; the nasty Alpine Linux OpenSSH flaw; Alpine’s GitLab near-miss; and the wide-open PHP2Shell security problem, which many groups still haven’t patched.

Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

"XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott.

McDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

The five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations.

Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently announced $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets.

Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks.

Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%.

Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East.

"We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," said Mehta.

Also, the analyst said that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty.

Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking. He highlighted that during Q2 2026, FANG's production volumes of 1,018 Mboe/d exceeded the high end of the company's guidance, driven by a stronger-than-expected natural gas output from Barnett development and improved downstream gas marketing.

Overall, Mehta is optimistic about Diamondback's growth and sees more upside in the stock, given higher production estimates, solid productivity and a deepening position in the Barnett shale formation. See Diamondback Energy Financials on TipRanks.

#3113. Forget Nvidia Stock at $160 per Share. Buy This Semiconductor ETF Instead.

Nvidia’s business is booming, but its headlines aren’t. Here’s a way to stay invested in AI chips without leaning on one company.

A month ago, Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%) was riding high as the dominant supplier of artificial intelligence (AI) chips. But wow, can things change fast in the stock market.

First, there was a sell-off in tech stocks, brought about by fears that spending was getting out of hand. Then the results of the midterm elections were seen to throw up roadblocks for data center approvals and construction. And finally, a scandal forced Nvidia founder Jensen Huang to resign, and investigators and Congress are probing the company's connections with a purported Chinese spy.

Now Nvidia is trading near $160, down 26% in the past month and 32% below its all-time high.

But there's an interesting disconnect here. Nvidia's business hasn't suddenly fallen apart. In fact, the company reported $96.2 billion in revenue in its fiscal 2027 second quarter, a whopping 106% increase from a year earlier. And big tech companies are expected to spend $800 billion on AI infrastructure this year, and more than $1 trillion next year.

Undoubtedly, there are plenty of opportunities in AI stocks. But if you want to limit your exposure to Nvidia and its bad headlines right now, a viable option is the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -0.34%). It might be the smartest investment you can make right now.

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF tracks the performance of the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor 25 index, which holds the largest and most liquid companies involved in chip production and equipment businesses that are listed on U.S. exchanges. Nvidia is the largest holding, at a little more than 17%. But the ETF also has several other companies at the forefront of AI-capable semiconductors -- including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Broadcom, and Advanced Micro Devices. These three companies collectively make up nearly 23% of SMH, which has 26 holdings total.

Data source: VanEck, YCharts (performance as of Nov. 13, 2026).

The most notable fact from the table above? Nvidia is the only member of SMH's top holdings that is in the red so far in 2026. And while Nvidia is down more than 12% for the year, SMH shows a 35% gain.

The ETF charges a reasonable 0.35% annual expense ratio, or $35 annually per $10,000 invested. And you get exposure to AI processors, memory, chipmaking equipment, and other semiconductor businesses.

The semiconductor industry has more going for it than one company, regardless of how dominant Nvidia has become. For investors who want to stay invested in AI without making a $160 bet on Nvidia's next chapter, SMH looks like the more attractive choice.

#3112. Google Pixel Tag Hands-On: Android Fans Get Their Own AirTag-Style Tracker

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Google's tracker has a few features we'd like to see Apple adopt.

If a company releases a product in an already established market, is it worth the effort? If you think I’m talking about Apple and Google, you’d be right – but this isn’t the iPhone Duo muscling into the folding phone fray. This time, the roles are reversed: Google has released the Pixel Tag, a small Bluetooth tracker that it hopes will be the Android ecosystem’s answer to Apple’s near-ubiquitous AirTag.

The Pixel Tag is available now for $30 each or $100 in a pack of four. It works with Android phones and uses Google’s Find Hub technology for tracking over distances beyond Bluetooth range. If you use an Android phone and have wanted the capability to track things such as keys, bags, bikes, vehicles and other indispensable items, and you want the tech to come from the company that designed the system, the Pixel Tag is an excellent choice.

It isn’t the first Android-compatible tracker. Motorola introduced its Moto Tag 2 earlier this year, and Tile has been the de facto AirTag alternative for several years. There’s also now a growing ecosystem of other items that tap into Apple’s Find My and Android’s Find Hub networks, ranging from slim credit-card-sized devices like the Rolling Square AirCard Pro and Peak Design’s Beacon Finder Card, to novel approaches like Falcam’s TagBatt, a battery for some Sony and Canon mirrorless cameras that integrates Apple Find My tracking.

Google jumping into this more crowded field tells me the company thinks there’s profit to be made by manufacturing its own hardware and software. It’s also investing in the infrastructure it’s already built out, and not leaving the hardware side to a constellation of other vendors.

Trackers like the Pixel Tag and AirTag can be a surprisingly deflating purchase: You pair them with your phone, put them into something you don’t want to lose track of – then forget about them. They’re usually not tactile the way a phone, watch or laptop is each day. And their value doesn’t kick into action until you think an item has gone missing.

After slinging AirTags into bags and dangling them off keychains, one thing I really appreciate about the Pixel Tag is its thinness. Apple chose a small, round footprint, even keeping the exact design for the second-generation AirTags. Google instead opted for a longer lozenge shape, at 1.8 inches (46.1mm), that is about two-thirds the height of the AirTag at 0.2 inch (5.4mm).

Google sent a Bellroy leather keychain as a sample accessory for review, and paired with the Pixel Tag, the two are a fine size for a pocket or clipped to an inside bag pocket. I thought the longer design would get in the way, but it’s not bad at all.

The Pixel Tag uses a CR2032 coin-sized battery that should last about a year (the same as the AirTag). It also has an IP67 rating, which is durable in 1 meter of water for up to 30 minutes.

Another departure from the AirTag is a physical button, making the Pixel Tag even more tactile. When you’re using Find Hub on your phone to locate it by sound, press once to stop the chirps it makes. Or, if you have the tag in hand (on a keychain, for example) and need to find your phone, press twice to ring the phone – it makes a pleasant sing-songy chime that gets louder and more intense as it continues, so I’m confident it’ll be easy to locate, even among couch cushions.

Speaking of the chimes, credit to the Google sound designers who came up with the Pixel Tag’s tune. It has three levels of loudness you can set, and seems plenty audible enough when you’re spelunking the living room for it. I measured it at 80 decibels, which when compared to the second-generation AirTag volume, is 7 less than the 87 decibels of Apple’s tracker.

One more nice touch compared to the AirTag: the Find Hub app shows the tag’s battery status. If that gets to Low or Very Low, the app sends you notifications every two weeks until the battery is replaced. After Apple showed battery statuses on AirTags in early versions of the Find My app, the company changed the Find My app so it only indicates battery when it’s low and needs to be replaced.

The best feature of either tracker is the ability to locate its exact location – not which building or room it’s in, but to tell if the item fell behind the couch or was accidentally dropped in the driveway. (Yes, I’m making up these examples from personal experience.)

Precision Finding uses a combination of Bluetooth 6.0 (via a feature called Channel Sounding) and the ultra-wideband chips inside the tag and the phone to directionally find the tracker when it’s within Bluetooth range. You hold the phone upright, perpendicular to the ground for the best connection. Then you wander your space, watching the indicator change as you get closer to the tag.

On the Pixel Tag, that indication is a wobbly circle shape that fills in as you get closer; when you’re on top of the tracker, the shape is fully filled. The Find Hub app also uses the camera and UWB chip to include an estimated distance in feet and inches (or meters and centimeters). When you’re close enough, the tracking shape becomes a directional arrow to point you the right way. UWB is compatible with the Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8 Fold and newer Pixel phones.

In my testing, the Find Nearby feature performed fairly well. Find Hub using a Pixel 11 Pro XL connected from within about 25 feet, including on multiple levels of a house when I was above or below it.

Perhaps because I was raised on science-fiction devices like the trackers in Aliens, though, I expected more consistent readings. There were times when both I and the tag remained stationary. The distance estimates would fluctuate by several feet.

Since I’ve had this review unit for only a few days, I haven’t yet had a chance to send it off with someone else and see if I can track it remotely using the Find Hub network. When nearby Android devices detect the Pixel Tag’s presence, they should securely and privately relay the tracker’s location to Google’s servers. (Apple’s Find My network operates the same way.) I’ll update this article once I’ve taken the tag on such an adventure.

Tracking all your stuff is invaluable – I learned this first-hand earlier this year when I left a small bag containing my passport in a hotel room, and was able to convince the hotel that the bag was still on the premises. But unfortunately, smart tags are being used to track people without their knowledge.

Google is taking the same approach as Apple to help thwart this type of tracking. If a tag is separated from the phone it’s paired with (or the phone of someone else you’ve chosen to share the tag location with), and the tag is moved, its chime activates.

The idea is that you’ll hear an unfamiliar chirp and investigate. It has an NFC chip that displays its information when you tap it using the NFC built into a phone.

Google and Xreal's spatial computing AR glasses have finally arrived and I've been wearing them for just a few days. They're an interesting hint at the future of both computing and wearables.

In the smart glasses space, there isn't anything like the Aura's. They're not quite a VR headset, but they're far more advanced than display glasses like Xreal's own One Pro Plus.

Xreal's only potential rivals exist in tech that has yet to actually hit shelves: the Snap Specs (which are supposed to ship "this fall") and the Meta VR Glasses that don't drop until sometime in Spring 2027.

There's a lot going on here, and we'll have a full review soon, but here are some early first impressions. As we dig into the glasses, if there's something you want to know reach out to scott.younker@futurenet.com or leave a comment below!

Beyond the puck, the Xreal Aura glasses won't look out of place next to any other display spectacles made by the company. There is an aesthetic to this kind of glasses and you can see it mirrored in Xreal's rival Viture with the recent Pro 2 glasses.

Where you'll notice the difference is in the cameras. Like the best smart glasses, the Aura features cameras at the temples plus one on the nose bridge. These are built to enable the gesture controls and 6DoF spatial computing, something no other Xreal glasses have natively.

The Aura sits somewhat between Meta's VR Glasses and Snap Specs; mostly, it comes down to software and cameras. Meta glasses have more cameras that can "see" your hands even if they're in your lap.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With the Aura's, moving your hands down to your lap means you're most likely using the puck as a trackpad, which works pretty well.

The puck is a computer for the glasses thanks to the powerful Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset. If you work in the Google suite, you have access to all of the Google apps and services you could want. Plus, it comes with Gemini AI, which you can access via voice controls.

Nicely, you don't need the puck for mirroring. You can connect the glasses to any device, save the Switch 2 (more on that below), and they will work like your normal Xreal glasses.

If you've worn a pair of Xreal glasses, the Aura feels about the same. I think they're fairly comfortable, and they do come with different nose pad sizes. Plus, the arms can be adjusted by three levels, which helps settle the glasses.

I want to highlight the speakers in the Aura. I hate speakers in display glasses and often find them tinny, preferring to use headphones. Also, especially since I travel or use the glasses to not disturb my partner at night even if the speakers are siloed, sound still leaks out.

Now, the Bose speakers in the Aura won't beat the best headphones, but they sound way better than any other glasses I've tested.

The included puck has both the computing chipsets and the battery. The puck is about the size of a thick iPhone 16, and does have some heft. You could use the included belt clip so that you don't have to hold the puck when you're out and about (which gives cellphone belt guy vibes).

The Xreal Aura are rated for about 3 hours of continuous use. I haven't done a full rundown test yet, but in my usage I've found that to be fairly accurate.

Perhaps that's for the best. I've found that the portion of the glasses that rests on your eyebrows gets warm. Not uncomfortably so, but noticeably enough that I wonder how that settles out over the long term. The puck, however, does seem to dissipate heat fairly well, and I never felt it get warm.

Xreal partnered with Google on the Aura and you can feel Mountain View's presence in the Android XR platform that lives in the puck. If you've ever tested the Samsung Galaxy XR headset, then you've seen the Android XR interface before.

It's the exact same here, with fewer capabilities thanks to fewer cameras and a little less power. The Aura also has a smaller FOV of 70 degrees. VR enthusiasts won't like that, but I think most people will find it more than usable.

You can use pinch gestures or the trackpad puck to control the interface. So far I've found the gesture controls smooth and intuitive. The Aura comes with a delightful setup process that teaches you how to use the gesture controls and puck so you can open the glasses up ready to go. It's honestly one of the better startup tutorials I've come across.

In previous hands-on sessions, the gesture controls felt a bit laggy at times, but whatever work Xreal and Google have done in the meantime has really made the controls much better.

Honestly, it's not as exciting as the eye-tracking in the Meta VR Glasses, but it works well, so I'm not knocking it too much.

Since the system runs on Android XR there are a lot of AR (and some VR-lite) games that you can play on the Aura. Xreal recommended the excellent Demeo, which is available in the Play Store.

I've already enjoyed Demeo in VR and the AR translation is a delight, using pinch controls to move the map, zoom in, and make choices. You'll need to pay attention to your hand position so the cameras can catch it.

I do think you'll need a controller to enjoy the most out of what the Aura can do or a mouse and keyboard. Fortunately, you can connect a surprising number of accessories to the Aura via Bluetooth (more on that below).

But what makes the Aura standout is the connectivity. As mentioned, you can just use the glasses to run a Steam Deck or mirror using a cable on your laptop. Have I been running WoW: Forever through the Aura glasses? Yes. Should I? That remains to be seen.

We got a sneak peek during AWE 2026 back in June, but the Xreal Aura is one of the few glasses that can connect to the Switch 2. Compared to the mini dock and larger pro dock that Viture makes, the Aura puck is lighter, smaller and does more than just act as a passthrough and battery pack. And it does so through the USB-C connection into the puck.

It's a delight to pop in Mario Kart World or the Ocarina of Time remake on the glasses. I still don't know how Xreal and Qualcomm got this to work, but I'm happy it does.

Xreal has said that you can accessorize the Aura with peripherals to enhance your use. With that in mind, the company did send us a wireless gaming controller built by GameSir, a wireless folding keyboard and a USB-C DP-in for mirroring external devices.

All three add an extra cost on top of the initial $1,299 glasses price. The GameSir controller costs $99 and can be used wirelessly or wired and has an AI button.

GameSir makes good controllers and the Xreal one is pretty decent. However, if you already have an Xbox, PlayStation or other Bluetooth controller, the Aura will support them. You won't have the Gemini button, but if you're like me and don't use that anyway, it shouldn't be a problem.

The Xreal keyboard is $79 but comes with Aura-specific keys in the FN row that enable you to control the glasses like you would your monitor on a laptop. It's actually a pretty comfortable keyboard, and the foldability for travel makes it an excellent companion. Honestly, so far you should add the $79 as part of the cost of getting a pair of Auras. You can also pair it with other devices, including laptops and tablets.

The cable is a Silkland USB-C one that costs $12.99. If you already have a USB-C DP in cable, it should work, but you're not out too much if you're looking to do wired mirroring.

At over $1,000, the Xreal Aura is pretty expensive, but these glasses are a lot of compute shrunk down into a pair of glasses and a cell phone-sized puck.

I don't know that everyone needs these glasses, and it's not quite the super portable laptop replacement yet, but it is an exciting glimpse at the future of AR glasses. Between the Aura, Snap Specs, and Meta VR Glasses the next generation of glasses has some true potential.

There's also room for the Aura to grow from both a software and hardware perspective.

We're not there yet, but the Aura feels like a true step toward the sci-fi eyewear that we saw in movies and shows as kids.

#3110. I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A new option called Memory summary lets you see and control the things that Gemini AI knows about you.

Like any AI, Google Gemini wants to remember things about you. The purported reason is to help tailor and personalize your conversations. But remember that your personal details may also wind up training the AI or even being reviewed by actual humans. With that in mind, you might want to find out just what Gemini knows about you. And now you can.

Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work

With a new option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time. These may be tidbits from your conversations or things that you directly told the AI. Even better, you can add or remove any details just by editing the memory or issuing your request directly to Gemini.

This new capability is available in Gemini across the board, so you can access it at the Gemini website, in the mobile iOS and Android apps, and in the Windows and Mac desktop apps.

Launch Gemini via the web or in one of the mobile or desktop apps. In the left pane displaying your previous chats, select the Settings icon at the bottom. At the Settings screen, select Personal Intelligence and then click or tap Memory summary. If the option is grayed out, it means the Memory feature is turned off. To proceed, turn it back on. You can always turn if off again afterward if you wish.

You’ll then see the individual details by category. My summary arranged the information across such categories as Essentials, Business & Career, Reading & Interests, and Culinary Preferences. Go down the list to see the individual items in each category. To view a recent history, tap the three dot-icon at the top and select Memory history. This shows you the latest changes and updates to Gemini’s memory.

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

What if Gemini’s memory includes details that are too personal or just incorrect? No problem. You can alter the AI’s memories of you. At the website or in one of the desktop apps, click the pencil icon at the top. Now you’re able to directly edit the text to add, remove, or revise specific details. After you’ve made your changes, just click Save.

For example, my summary said that I lived in Madison County. I have no idea where Gemini got that notion, as I live in New York. Here, I revised the text and saved the changes, which then synced across the Gemini website and apps.

The mobile apps have no direct editing capability. But there’s another method that works both on mobile and on the desktop. Just tell Gemini what change you want to make. At the prompt, type and speak your request, and the AI will carry it out for you.

As an example, my summary said that I run a business called Batter Up selling collectible baseball cards. That’s not at all true. I had once referred to such a store only to test Gemini’s image creation skills to design a logo for a baseball card seller. Here, I simply told Gemini that I don’t run a business called Batter Up and asked it to remove that item from its memory. Poof, that detail quickly disappeared.

#3109. Could This Under-the-Radar, Cash-Rich Stock Be a 10-Bagger By 2030?

The neighborhood network is growing again, but a 10-fold return would require a lot to go right.

I won't sugarcoat it. Nextdoor (NXDR +0.58%) has been a tough investment to own since it went public in 2021 at $10 per share. The stock is down roughly 80% since then, and for a while it wasn't clear that the neighborhood social network could grow at all, at least profitably.

That's starting to change. Users are coming back, the company is close to breaking even, and it has a large cash cushion relative to its size. With a market value of about $790 million, it's fair to ask whether Nextdoor could be a 10-bagger from here. Here's the bull case, and the hurdles.

In the third quarter, Nextdoor's revenue rose 14% year over year, ahead of expectations. Platform weekly active users also grew by 14% to a record 24.5 million, the third straight quarter of sequential growth. What's more, management said the growth came mostly from returning users and product improvements, not paid marketing, and the number of people posting each week rose 27%.

CEO and co-founder Nirav Tolia believes Nextdoor is uniquely positioned to thrive in the AI age. In a world where more of the internet is becoming synthetic, he argues, real people verified to a real place become scarce. That's a compelling angle as AI-generated content floods the rest of social media. But could the stock be a 10-bagger for investors who buy at these levels?

In the third quarter, Nextdoor's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) more than doubled to $10.3 million, and Nextdoor's net loss shrank to less than $1 million. It's worth noting that GAAP results still benefit from interest income on the more than $380 million in cash on its balance sheet, and that stock-based compensation remains high at 18% of revenue. The former adds to the bottom line, while the stock-based comp is the main reason Nextdoor is yet to achieve GAAP profitability.

Speaking of cash, the balance sheet is a major strength. Nextdoor ended the quarter with $382 million in cash and investments and no debt. That's nearly half of its market value, and the company has a $100 million buyback program in place to take advantage of weakness in the stock price

To be sure, a 10x return from Nextdoor would mean a market value of roughly $8 billion. If the market valued Nextdoor at about 5 times sales, a reasonable valuation for a profitable social platform, that would require roughly $1.6 billion in annual revenue, or a little more than five times this year's expected $294 million.

That's where the bull case runs into trouble. Average revenue per user rose just 1% last quarter. Nextdoor's audience is growing faster than its ability to monetize it, and it competes with much larger platforms for local advertising dollars. As a small-cap stock, it can also be volatile. However, the top-line growth has been accelerating, and if the company can figure out how to improve monetization, a 10x isn't outside the realm of possibilities.

In fairness, getting to $1.6 billion in revenue by 2030 might be pushing it, even if things go well. But this is a small company with tremendous upside potential if management can figure out profitable long-term growth (and the signs since Tolia returned as CEO have been mostly positive). After all, Nextdoor could 10x from its current price and have a smaller market cap than either Snap (SNAP +7.37%) or Pinterest (PINS -0.11%). Plus, keep in mind that if the company gets aggressive with its buyback program at the current level, it could reduce the share count and help drive per-share value.

Having said all that, Nextdoor is more interesting today than it's been in years. It has a unique asset in 15 years of verified local conversations, its users are growing again, and its cash pile gives it time to figure out monetization. I own Nextdoor and like what I've been seeing in recent quarters, and I think it's just a matter of time before the market starts to appreciate the company's positive momentum.

#3108. Five iOS 27 Toggles That Make Your iPhone Easier to Read and More Private

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

Whether it’s a new iPhone or an updated one, these five iOS 27 settings are worth checking before you settle in.

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo ship with iOS 27’s default settings, and so does any older iPhone that updated this fall. Those defaults include a strong Liquid Glass effect, automatic subtitles on videos and a Siri that saves and syncs your conversations.

They’re easy to change once you know where to look. Here are five settings worth adjusting, whether you’re setting up a new phone or finally getting around to it on your current one.

Read more: Win a New Apple Watch in CNET Big Guessing Game Contest

Apple introduced Liquid Glass with iOS 26, giving menus, buttons, notifications and other interface elements a translucent appearance. Not everyone was a fan of the new design, and with iOS 27, you now get more control over exactly how transparent the interface looks.

Go to Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass. Drag the slider to the right to add more tint and opacity, making buttons and text easier to distinguish from whatever is behind them. Moving it left makes the interface more transparent.

If the most opaque setting still isn’t enough, go to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and turn on Reduce Transparency. This makes translucent backgrounds more solid across iOS, although it overrides the regular Liquid Glass appearance controls.

More tint makes Liquid Glass easier to read.

The new Siri AI works similarly t ChatGPT or Claude in iOS 27. It now comes complete with a dedicated app where you can revisit previous conversations. Those chats sync through iCloud so you can start a conversation on your iPhone and continue it on another Apple device, such as your Mac.

By default, iOS 27 keeps those conversations forever, but there is a way to automatically get rid of older conversations if you don’t want them piling up.

If you don’t need a permanent archive of everything you ask Siri, go to Settings > Siri > Keep Conversations and choose 30 Days or 1 Year. Selecting either option permanently deletes conversations beyond that timeframe.

Siri keeps your conversations forever unless you choose a shorter limit.

While you’re there, tap Opens To and select A New Conversation if you want the Siri app to open with a blank chat instead of showing your recent conversations every time.

Siri AI requires an iPhone 15 Pro or 15 Pro Max, iPhone Air or an iPhone 16 or later.

iOS 27 puts a new Write with Siri button above the keyboard in apps including Messages, Mail and Notes. You can ask Siri AI to draft something from scratch, proofread what you’ve written or rewrite it in a different tone.

The thing is, I’m not a big fan of the AI writing tools, so I don’t use them at all.

Screen Time lets you completely disable Siri’s writing tools.

This disables access to the writing tools across your iPhone, rather than simply hiding the keyboard button, so only do this if you don’t use Apple’s AI writing tools at all. You can return to the same menu and choose Allow if you want them back. Apple documents the restriction under its Apple Intelligence Screen Time controls.

Introduced back in iOS 17, Siri can now wake up when you simply say “Siri” instead of “Hey Siri.” The one-word command is convenient, but it also makes accidental activations more likely whenever someone says Siri’s name in a conversation or a video they’re watching online.

Siri goes absolutely bonkers whenever I’m in work meetings about Apple features.

To disable the feature, go to Settings > Siri > Talk to Siri. Choose “Hey Siri” instead of “Siri.”

Requiring “Hey Siri” can help prevent accidental activations.

You’ll still be able to bring up Siri with your voice, but the extra word makes it less likely to wake up when you aren’t talking to it directly.

This isn’t exclusive to iOS 27, but it’s been annoying me more recently, so thought I would throw it in here, especially with Siri AI being the prominent feature on this update.

iOS 27 now automatically shows subtitles on videos in Photos, Safari and other apps that use Apple’s video player. I don’t mind captions when I need them, but they can take up too much of the video and distract me from whatever I’m watching.

They don’t appear randomly though. By default, iOS can turn them on when the video is in another language, when your iPhone is muted or when you skip back.

Whenever subtitles appear in Apple’s video player, you can tap the video to show the playback controls, tap the More Controls button, select Subtitles and choose Off.

If iOS keeps turning them on because it thinks the video is in another language, go to Settings > Accessibility > Subtitles & Captioning. Under Automatic Subtitles, turn off When Languages Don’t Match.

The same menu also has switches for Show When Muted and Show on Skip Back, so you can disable those behaviors individually without turning off every automatic subtitle feature.

You can also disable each automatic subtitle trigger individually.

Some apps and websites use their own video players, so you may need to find a separate CC or subtitles button instead.

For more on iOS 27, check out this article on the features it brings to your iPhone and how Siri AI helped one of my colleagues avoid eating diarrhea lettuce.

#3107. AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Rapidly advancing AI models are making it cheaper and easier to uncover critical vulnerabilities, but it's a double-edged sword - and a gift to hackers.

The best AI models on the market couldn’t find zero-days earlier this year, but now they can in less than 15 minutes and at a cost of a few bucks, according to a new report from penetration testing firm Xint.io. The findings raise questions about how vulnerabilities will be discovered and exploited in the future.

Every major AI developer is working at breakneck speed to improve model effectiveness. At the same time, token prices continue to fall, with studies showing that the average cost of tokens, which varies by domain, has dropped by about 47% per quarter since 2023 and 15% last month alone, due to intense competition among companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

This is good news for businesses trying to harness AI for productivity and new services, but as token prices fall, it has also become cheaper for attackers to launch AI-assisted attacks, including software breaches caused by exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

A report published by Xint.io examines how popular AI models have evolved over the past year to the point where cybersecurity tasks that would have failed only months ago now succeed. The team analyzed seven models launched since February 2026: two from OpenAI, three from Anthropic, and two open-source models from DeepSeek and Z.ai. The team tracked, over time, how they performed in finding a target vulnerability.

The target of this research was a security flaw in Google’s V8 engine. Tracked as CVE-2026-102321, the type confusion bug leading to remote code execution (RCE) was disclosed to the Google Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) by Xint researcher Taisic Yun and so was not present in the AI models’ training datasets.

The research scope was limited to a set of source files, including the file containing the vulnerability, and each model was instructed to search for security issues within these files.

Xint’s first test was conducted in February. After 25 hours and $350 of scanning, the best models then available still couldn’t find the critical vulnerability.

In July, GPT 5.6 Sol found the zero-day flaw for $22 in 44 minutes.

Also: Finding Linux bugs is easy – fixing them is another story

By September, GPT 6 Sol discovered the bug in 13 minutes for only $4.24 with its first guided prompt.

Only three of the seven models found the bug: GPT 6 Sol, GPT 5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5, all launched from July onward. GPT 5.6 Sol needed two prompts, while Claude Opus 5 found it on its first try but at a higher cost of $43.40.

DeepSeek’s and Z.ai’s models failed the task.

The researchers say that the combination of AI model development and low token prices means that “mediocre hackers” can now use frontier models effectively to discover and potentially exploit vulnerabilities, and “while we are still far from complete amateurs using unharnessed models to hack systems and applications, what used to be considered too hard and costly to be worth the effort of the average hacker is now reachable.”

As a result, organizations need to adjust their security posture accordingly — but falling token costs and evolving AI skills and speed can also work in your favor.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac

There’s nothing stopping an organization’s security team or pentesters from running the same checks themselves to find vulnerabilities before threat actors do. AI-assisted tests, arguably, are no longer something that can be pushed back to next year’s budgetary review. By performing a risk assessment that focuses on likely weak spots, such as public-facing services or a digital supply chain that hasn’t been audited for years, organizations can mitigate the risk AI-enabled cyberattacks pose.

Zero-day vulnerabilities are unknown to vendors, and a patch might not be available when they go public or are actively exploited in the wild. So, AI can only go so far, but it can free up your defenders for tasks that need the human touch. Furthermore, maintaining zero-trust access controls, segmenting and shoring up your network’s defenses, and monitoring endpoints for signs of suspicious behavior can do as much as, or more than, AI.

As Xint notes, “expertise still matters” when it comes to instructing AI models to discover vulnerabilities. In some cases, the models couldn’t find the target vulnerability without guidance, so additional runs were needed, increasing time and cost.

“Software breaches still require some level of technical proficiency,” the researchers say, “but no longer top-of-the-distribution expertise.”

#3105. Samsung Galaxy S27 Lineup Could Have a Personal AI Assistant Built-In

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Galaxy Claw could make calls and send text messages for you.

Samsung is expected to unveil its Galaxy S27 lineup early next year, and a personal AI assistant might be arriving as well. The so-called Galaxy Claw could perform a variety of functions, including making phone calls, sending text messages and creating appointments, according to Android Authority.

The tech news website discovered Galaxy Claw while digging into Samsung’s Personal Agent Core app, which is a new AI system that connects AI across Samsung apps and Google services. This new system can also pull data from your calendar, Gmail, text messages, delivery info and other sources and also autonomously perform tasks upon your instructions.

Android Authority said that coding details for the Personal Agent Core app were shared by The Cipher Project, a Telegram channel that often leaks Samsung software updates, One UI features and unreleased device functions.

A representative for Samsung did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Samsung has had AI functionality on its phones and other devices since January 2024, when the company introduced Galaxy AI. The main capabilities at that launch included Circle to Search — allowing users to search for anything on the screen — as well as live language translation and photo editing.

Over the past two-plus years, Samsung has integrated more AI functionality into its devices, including Google Gemini and Gemini Live. Although Samsung devices have plenty of AI to do things for you, it primarily operates on your command rather than acting as an autonomous agent.

The new Galaxy Claw system might launch at Samsung Unpacked in January or February, when Samsung could release the Galaxy S27 series, which could include the Ultra flagship. Samsung has not officially announced what products it will launch at Unpacked.

According to Android Authority, the Galaxy Claw could connect to various apps on your phone and perform functions for you. Those apps could include Calendar, Contacts, Gallery, Gmail, Messages, Notifications, Perplexity, Phone and Voice Recorder.

So, in essence, the Claw could create appointments, write and send emails and make phone calls. For example, you could have Claw set up a meeting and send calendar notifications to the attendees with an attached agenda. Or perhaps Claw could call someone for you to tell them where you’re going.

Android Authority said other components could be included — Daily Brief, Device Cleaner, Travel Planner and a dedicated widget.

Those tasks would be a major step up from what Galaxy AI can currently do on Samsung phones — live translation, text drafting, photo editing, scam call detection and more.

Adding agentic AI won’t justify the $1,400 or even $1,500 price tag for the S27 Ultra but could help generate customer loyalty, says tech reviewer Jon Rettinger.

“People buy the Ultra for the camera, the screen and the S Pen, and that won’t change next year,” Rettinger told CNET. “Where an agent could matter is keeping people. If Galaxy Claw is reading my Gmail, my calendar and my texts and quietly handling the busywork, switching phones gets a lot harder, because I’d be walking away from an assistant that knows how my week runs.”

Rettinger said Samsung would be wise to include the Galaxy Claw with the new devices and not as a separate subscription service.

“So, now the pitch is $1,500 for the phone, then a monthly fee for the feature that’s supposed to justify the phone,” Rettinger said. “That’s a tough sell. If Samsung wants this to move hardware, it should come included on the Ultra.”

People apparently will maintain authority and control over Galaxy Claw, according to Android Authority. The new system would request access to sensitive data such as contacts, photos and calendar events, as well as permission to execute functions such as sending text messages and making calls. The Claw wouldn’t go rogue on you, in other words.

Samsung users might also be able to schedule the Claw to do tasks and functions regularly. Perhaps you need to email or text weekly reminders to someone about something. You could instruct the AI on the task and when to do it each week. It might only require a simple prompt from you, such as, “Please remind my son to take out the garbage by 8 a.m. Monday mornings.”

Android Authority said tasks could be scheduled by hour, day, weekly and custom intervals. Users would also be able to cancel or modify scheduled tasks and check task history.
